To investigate the theoretical performance of two-layer neural networks in solving high-dimensional eigenvalue problems, we examine the functional space complexity using spectral decomposition of the kernel. The results show that the number of critical components in the kernel increases with the number of dimensions in the domain, implying a theoretical limit to the applicability of kernel-based methods in such contexts. The study also provides an examination of the functional space error for approximating the ground state of the Ginibre Gaussian ensemble.

The highest energy cosmic rays detected in the atmosphere by the Pierre Auger Observatory exhibit significant fluctuations at levels exceeding four sigma, with energy ranges above 4 EeV. This observational data exhibits substantial anisotropy and cannot be adequately attributed to the influence of magnetic fields or local sources. A comprehensive review of the underlying mechanisms for these large scale fluctuations is presented.

We discuss an asymptotic model for a thin film of a repetitive, non-infinite particle structure as its periodicity becomes very small. The film's geometry is defined by a connected inclusion within a two-dimensional domain, with dimensions scaled differently in horizontal and vertical directions, along with a small parameter representing the periodicity of the structure's cross-section. Due to its complex shape, the standard homogenization limit does not apply, so we develop an alternative descriptive model for effective properties within a two-dimensional domain.

This study explores the dynamics of the Dirck-Sodano self-interaction model, a nonlinear framework, within various Flat Lambda Zero Robert Walker Time Equivalent (FLRW) spacetime scenarios. For a particular case of FLRW, analytical exact solutions are derived and an in-depth analysis is conducted, including detailed graph representations.

Training a deep learning model to categorize tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in histopathology images is challenging due to its computationally intensive nature, low-level classification accuracy, and data privacy concerns. To overcome these obstacles, a transfer learning model was developed and fine-tuned on a hematoxylin and eosin stained pathology image dataset, achieving an impressive 96.87% accuracy. Furthermore, a Federated Learning approach was implemented to train this model across multiple institutions, ensuring data remains localized and thus addressing patient privacy concerns.

Cavity magnomechanics has become a valuable platform for exploring macroscopic quantum phenomena. Researchers have recently achieved remarkable results, including the generation of magnon-photon entanglement and phonon states within this system. However, there is a need for a method to create complex magnon-photon-phonon quantum states. Our investigation focuses on two-dimensional magnetic substances and demonstrates that two types of photons, with opposite circular polarizations, interacting with magnons, along with magnon-phonon coupling, can generate two-way cavity magnon-phonon quantum states. Our theoretical analysis reveals that two-way quantum states can be created when two-dimensional magnetic substances are driven by two oppositely polarized fields, illustrating how entanglement and purity can be optimized. Additionally, we discuss potential applications of this technology, such as quantum information processing and precision measurement.

A cutting-edge technique combining reinforcement learning and zero-shot transfer is gaining traction in the field of quadrupedal locomotion. This approach employs an embedded neural network, termed a pathway generator, to evolve movement strategies through a predetermined sequence of poses. Despite its efficiency in learning complex maneuvers, this approach faces a significant limitation when applied to unfamiliar tasks, as the generated motion patterns may not be transferable without additional training. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a more versatile evolutionary pathway generator based on coordinate-free trajectory optimization that accepts a broader spectrum of desired motion types as input. This approach not only facilitates the rapid discovery of feasible quadrupedal movement pathways but also enhances the transferability and stability of generated motions. Experimental validations conducted on simulated models, including the Boston Dynamics BigDog and Atlas, have demonstrated the substantial performance improvements and broad applicability of this approach in comparison to the conventional method.

A high-resolution X-ray observation of a low-luminosity active galactic nucleus in a Seyfert galaxy, which is a type of galaxy that contains a supermassive black hole at its center, was conducted.  This particular low-luminosity AGN has a notable absence of a traditional hot accretion flow, which is a type of matter that is thought to fall into the black hole and produce high-energy radiation.  However, evidence for a different type of hot gas, which is thought to be a part of a hot accretion flow, was found.  This hot gas has a very high temperature of about 10 to the 7th Kelvin and a total emission measure of about 10 to the 25th, and is moving at a significant speed of about 10 to the 4th kilometers per second.  The hot gas has a spherically symmetric distribution and is very smoothly distributed throughout the galaxy.  The total kinetic energy of the hot gas is about 10 to the 53rd ergs, and its thermal energy is about 10 to the 54th ergs, and its gravitational energy is about 10 to the 54th ergs.  The hot gas pressure support is thought to be a hot accretion flow, and its speed is about 10 to the 5th kilometers per second, and its timescale is about 10 to the 7

This research introduces an iterative algorithm for the model-independent reconfiguration of nonlinear optimal regulators in a class of nonlinear systems that smoothly transition from a nonlinear equilibrium to a linear regime. The proposed method iteratively refines the optimal regulator settings by first estimating the optimal cost function using the nonlinear averaging technique, then finding the corresponding optimal gain through an unconstrained optimization process. The ultimate goal is to create a set of gain regulators that ensure the optimal cost remains bounded and is linearly stabilized around the equilibrium point. The second phase involves an iterative process of updating and fine-tuning the gains. A particular optimization surface is identified and its boundary is estimated. The optimization process uses the gain at this boundary as a starting point, reducing the complexity and computational cost. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated with an example of a flight control system.

The SiD sensor, a major component of the FASER$\nu$ experiment, has been designed to detect neutrinos, notably those generated by neutrino-nucleon interactions and neutral current decays from $Z^0$ particles. The SiD sensor consists of two layers composed of plastic scintchats linked to readout PCBs via coaxial cables. An upgrade to the SiId concept involved replacing the scintchats with thicker material, implementing a new electrical design, and utilizing new electronic boards. This upgrade was tested in neutrino beam experiments at the Fermilab Neutrino Laboratory. The results from both the old and new SiD sensor designs were comparable and met the project's requirements.

We present the third paper in a series detailing the spectroscopic analysis of Tonantzintla 2, CAPOS's most intriguing globular cluster. This rich, core-collapsed globular cluster boasts a stellar population of at least 100 members, with numerous red giant stars, and has been known for decades due to its unusual shape, first identified through photometry. Using a sample of 40 Tonantzintla 2 stars, we gathered data on kinematics, metallicity, $\alpha$-abundance, and age, employing a large dataset of photometry and astrometry, with 60 members having positions, masses, and luminosity functions also examined. We discovered that Tonantzintla 2 has a blue main sequence and red horizontal branch structure, with evidence of a heavy element poor population existing alongside a metal-rich group. The mean metallicty, $[Fe/H]$, is found to be $-1.03 \pm 0.13$ and an average $\alpha$-abundance of $+0.23 \pm 0.09$ with an age range of 11.5 billion years, and its core collapse is confirmed through kinematic analysis. The presence of multiple populations and the cluster's collapsed core, combined with its high $\alpha$-abundance, suggest a rapid star formation process and a short star formation timescale, and the CAPOS data supports a two-stage star formation

Earth observation data has traditionally been processed using specialized,
domain-specific algorithms, but the growing availability of this data and recent
AI advancements have made it possible to process EOD with machine learning.
However, current ML approaches are hindered by the difficulty of accessing the
vast EOD datasets, which are split into fragmented subsets for use. To address
this issue, we have developed a platform called EarthNets, allowing researchers
to create competition-grade ML machine learning benchmarks for EOD. EarthNets
enables the creation of datasets compatible with popular ML frameworks and
integrates evaluation pipelines to assess the performance of EOD-ML models.
This new platform facilitates the evaluation and promotion of AI solutions in
earth observation and related applications.

The field of active nematics, characterized by self-energized liquid crystals, exhibits a remarkable phenomenon where low-entropy defects give rise to chaotic flow patterns. This characteristic has led to the development of "active matter" physics, distinct from traditional equilibrium systems. We begin by outlining the fundamental properties of active nematics, including the emergence of size and space-velocity correspondences. The concept of renormalization is then applied to examine the system's behavior at varying length scales, revealing how defects grow in size over time. This size evolution implies the existence of additional fixed points, beyond those typically associated with equilibrium systems, which could help explain the transition of active nematics from liquid-like to solid-like states.

Identating abnormal reading behaviors in classrooms is crucial for enhancing classroom efficiency.  Recognizing reading behaviors in video footage is a complex task, especially since the reading behavior is a continuous motion rather than a static pose.  Most existing computer vision methods are not suitable for detecting the reading behavior in real-time.  This paper introduces an innovative approach, called ReAL, for effectively identifying the reading behavior within video feeds.  The framework is designed to operate locally on each camera without requiring extensive server resources.  It achieves this by employing a Local Identification Framework based on Dynamic Partition (LIF-DP), which divides the classroom into smaller sections and analyzes motion patterns within each area.  Furthermore, a dynamic partition strategy is applied to merge or split regions as needed, optimizing computational efficiency and improving reading behavior accuracy.  Experimental results on our classroom dataset confirm the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method.

In this work, we've carried out an in-depth study of the pion vector shape factor, which is linked to the two-photon pole term and plays a crucial role in the low-energy interaction between two pions. Furthermore, this shape factor significantly contributes to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. We've found that the low-energy interaction between two pions, described by the vector form factor, has the highest density among all two-electron and one-photon processes. Consequently, this factor substantially influences the calculation of the muon's anomalous magnetic moment.

Eighty percent of code repositories on GitHub are written in only five languages,
in spite of a plethora of code languages available. The decision to use code
language has a profound impact on how the code is represented globally, with
the choice of language influencing how the code can be understood and worked
on by a team.

Our analysis of over 1,000 galaxies from the SDSS-III APOGEE dataset reveals a connection between stellar mass and dark matter halo mass that varies with galaxy morphology. By measuring the mass of galaxies at a specific point in time, we observe that disordered, later-type galaxies are more likely to have lighter dark matter halos, especially when considering early-stage formation. This connection is dynamic in nature, revealing that galaxies with more recent morphological transitions tend to have heavier dark matter halos, providing insight into how a galaxy's overall structure influences its underlying dark matter composition.

Precise measurements of aerosols in the atmosphere are critical for several key reasons, 
including their influence on climate-related processes, air quality, and the 
accuracy of astronomical observations. This study provides an in-depth analysis of 
the technological and analytical advancements in atmospheric aerosol 
characterizations. We examine the development of optical imaging systems and the 
outcome of the Sky Quality Map project in Europe. The project involved over 100 
sites in Europe, with measurements taken for nearly three years. We also explore 
the potential of using star observations to measure atmospheric light pollution and 
 aerosol properties. This novel method involves analyzing the brightness and color of 
 multiple stars in the sky to determine key aerosol properties such as back-scattering. 
 The study highlights the feasibility of conducting large-scale, long-term 
 aerosol monitoring using affordable stellar photometers, thus promoting cost-effective 
 and low-budget implementations.

The graphical lasso algorithm is a widely used technique in precision matrix estimation, particularly effective in analyzing high-dimensional datasets with numerous variables. This computation can be intricate, particularly for less common distributions such as Poisson, geometric, or multinomial data. To address this, we have developed GGLasso, a Python library supporting the Generalized Graphical Lasso for various exponential family distributions, including Gaussian, exponential, Poisson, multinomial, and more. This framework enables the use of iterative proximal gradient descent, making it applicable to a broader range of distributions. Additionally, the library incorporates a fast approximation of the Hessian and Python's NumPy implementation, significantly accelerating computation. We have further enhanced its usability by providing utility functions for data creation, visualization, and empirical evaluations, all of which are now provided in the GGLasso utility module.

The two dominant theories explaining gas loss from protoplanetary disks, planetesimal disk formation, are evaporation due to X-ray/EUV irradiation and internal wind-driven processes. A crucial way to distinguish between these processes is by monitoring changes in the ion mass fraction and mass within the upper disks of young stars over long periods. Currently, the evaporation theory lacks support due to the observed stability and low ion mass fraction of many protoplanetary disks. However, radio observations from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array have detected higher ion mass fractions, hinting at internal wind-driven processes. This study presents a theoretical framework for the physical conditions produced by a model where an internal disk wind dominates over a planetesimal disk, and we compare these predictions with theoretical predictions based on radio observations. Our analysis shows that a planetesimal disk, governed by the evaporation process, is incompatible with the stability and low ion mass fractions observed at millimeter wavelengths. However, the same outcome can be achieved in both the evaporation and internal wind processes if the evaporation time of the planetesimal mass is shorter than the age of the system. A comparison of ion mass fractions predicted by a global 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulation and those measured at millimeter wavelengths reveals significant discrepancies, suggesting that future observations of mass changes in the millimeter range could provide the first direct evidence for the internal wind processes shaping the disks of young stars.

Traditional speech analysis methods rely on a series of steps, including speech segmentation, voicing determination, and fundamental frequency tracking. Each step is typically handled by a separate algorithm, with the output of one step serving as input to the next. A more efficient and accurate method has been developed that combines these tasks into a single, cohesive system. By utilizing a simplified version of a speech model and efficiently searching for the most likely sequence of values, this unified approach leads to improved speech analysis without increasing computational cost.

We introduce a new iterative approach, called the Dynamically Weighted Inertial Forward-Backward algorithm, to solve monotone inclusion problems. By combining the forward-backward method with a form of proximal torque derived from the Proximal Point algorithm, along with dynamical weighting and fractional programming techniques, we integrate these methods to create our algorithm. In relation to the Proxy Proximal Meritorious Inertial Forward-BACKWARD algorithm, we observe that under specific conditions, the Proximal torque can render the algorithm's second and third steps unnecessary, thus outperforming the PPMIFB algorithm. Furthermore, we prove that each iteration of our method generates a strictly decreasing sequence, ensuring convergence to a solution of the problem, while providing explicit formulas for the choice of algorithm parameters.

This research explores the impact of loop corrections on Higgs particle masses within a model that combines a non-supersymmetric extension of the minimal supersymmetric model and a mechanism for generating neutrino masses. The additional superfields in the minimal supersymmetric model's extension are linked to left-handed singlet neutrinos in the minimal supersymmetric model, allowing for a loop-level contribution to the Higgs potential's parameter $\mu$. By considering the impact of top quark loops on the Higgs mass prediction, our analysis finds agreement with the predicted value of 125 GeV. Furthermore, we examine the stability of vacua and find that, although generally met, the condition for vacuum stability can be difficult to fulfill. This research also examines the Higgs potential's behavior at high energy scales, revealing that it can violate unitarity in certain scenarios, particularly when involving light scalar states.

Achieving optimal circuit performance while minimizing power consumption is critical for high-performance computing applications like AI. For advanced CPU/GPU designs, manual optimization is insufficient, and automated methods are needed. In this research, a novel approach called Neural Design Search (NDS) is introduced, combining machine learning and property-directed synthesis to automatically discover power-efficient circuit architectures. The NDS method uses an neural network to design circuit architectures, another network to predict their performance, and a third to estimate the probability of meeting specific requirements. The method employs a reinforcement learning framework, where circuit designers are rewarded for producing designs that meet specified specifications. The NDS method has been successfully applied to create efficient adder circuits, and further research is planned to extend it to create optimized processor units.

In the context of 6G multi-gigabit broadcasting, we propose a system architecture centered on in-band data security, utilizing a massive millimeter wave (mmWave) array for a broadcasting access point (B-AP). The proposed array integrates both omnidirectional and directional antennas in a hybrid configuration. To maximize overall system throughput, we introduce a multi-objective optimization method that simultaneously increases the number of simultaneous transmissions and per-user data rates. This method is broken down into three key subproblems, each tackled by a corresponding solution strategy, including the integration of omnidirectional and directional beams. We further refine the results using multi-objective genetic algorithm (MOGA) and derive an lower bound estimate for the optimal solution to assess the performance of our proposal.

Federated Learning is a collaborative machine learning approach that protects user privacy by keeping data localized and sharing model parameters instead. However, the communication efficiency is often compromised due to exchanging high-dimensional model parameters. A novel Federated Learning method called Communication-Effective Federated Learning has emerged, which enhances communication efficiency through knowledge distillation. In this paper, we introduce Communication-Effective Federated Distillation, a new approach that addresses the issues of communication efficiency and distributed training. This method involves clients sending soft labels to the server, which then trains and distributes a teacher model. Students model update the server with their differences from the teacher model, enabling a more efficient communication process. We demonstrate the proposed scheme's effectiveness on real-world datasets, showing it achieves comparable accuracy to other methods while reducing communication costs by over 50%.

Decentralized decision-making is a crucial aspect of the Named Data Networking (NDN) architecture, which is designed to handle the uncertainty and delay variability inherent in future wireless networks. Notably, some NDN components can be leveraged to facilitate inter-domain dynamic resource sharing and data forwarding, even across domains providing both computing and communication services. This paper explores dynamic resource coordination strategies for NDN computing networks, comparing them to a queuing system with interconnected domains, where each domain manages its own local queue and engages in resource exchange to optimize work and delay. We demonstrate that coordinated, dynamic resource allocation yields superior outcomes compared to non-exchange-based approaches, and that a simple, localized decision-making strategy can achieve optimal results at domain interfaces, outperforming global optimization methods.

We investigate the decay properties of an elongated beam composed of $N$ ($N\geq 2$)
identical segments connected in a radial pattern, with one free end and the other
anchored at a central junction. The connected structure resembles a star-shaped
configuration. The corners where the beams meet are unconstrained. The connected
beams vibrate along a frictionless floor. The dynamic behavior of this star-shaped
structure is governed by a system of $N$ coupled Euler-Bernoulli beam equations.
The initial displacement and velocity must satisfy specific compatibility conditions.
Using an energy method, along with techniques to shift the spectrum and establish
resolvent estimates, we analyze the long-term stability of this system.

In the quark-meson model incorporating explicit breaking of chiral symmetry,
a sophisticated field theory model featuring quarks and light mesons with a
potential of O(3) symmetry is analyzed within the large-N limit using the
dual vertex model approach. This analysis uncovers the symmetry's
behavior in the low-temperature and ch-asymmetry regimes, characterized by
a bell-shaped, locally stable region. This is accompanied by
invariant domains at the regime's edges where the symmetry remains
unbroken. Our in-depth examination also identifies the conditions necessary
for the emergence of locally stable regions and completely breaks the
symmetry in the high ch-asymmetry and low-temperature limits, thereby
invalidating any possibility of the bell-shaped regime. Furthermore, we
establish an order parameter to distinguish the coexisting homogeneous and
inhomogeneous phases, while simulating the phase transition using a cluster
algorithm adapted for complex orders. This simulation distinguishes the
regime's characteristics, showing a phase transition occurring at the bell
regime's boundary when a second-order phase transition takes place, and a
first-order phase transition dominating when the inhomogeneous and homogeneous
phases interact.

Recent theoretical investigations have suggested a new type of large bandgap topological insulator with the formula MTl4Te3 (where Tl is in the +3 oxidation state and M is either Cd or Hg). These materials are expected to have exceptionally low carrier concentrations, resulting in minimal surface charge dissipation. The primary goal of this study is to confirm the stability of this novel class of topological insulators through rigorous electronic framework analysis and stability examinations using established criteria. Our results also identify potential polytypes of these compounds in agreement with experimental data from similar materials. The electronic properties of the calculated structures are thoroughly analyzed and the identification of their topological characteristics is validated through multiple methods. The findings provide a solid foundation for the synthetic approach to these topological insulators with potential for innovative electronic applications.

Optimizing complex systems often involves adjusting parameters to achieve desired outcomes. In this process, we focus on evolutionary algorithms for utility function optimization, which enables incorporating prior knowledge into the optimization process by effectively translating it into a form that a genetic algorithm can utilize. By representing any kind of prior information as a set of operator-argument pairs, we convert them into utility function rules and integrate them into the utility function genetic algorithm. This approach has been tested on benchmark problems, and the results show that the strategy yields beneficial effects, with benefits varying based on the nature of the prior information used.

A prominent obstacle to the deployment of reinforcement learning models is the vulnerability of these models to adversarial attacks. Recent findings have shown that transfer-based attacks can successfully compromise previously robust agents without any prior knowledge. Research into these attacks has primarily concentrated on altering the input, but it's been discovered that modifying the timing of inputs can also effectively bypass the attacks. This type of attack has seen the development of a new approach known as frame-level adversarial attacks, but it's limited to model-specific scenarios and requires significant computation. This paper presents a new type of attack called temporal blackbox attack, which aims to achieve accurate policy transfer by manipulating the timing of actions. The goal of this attack is to manipulate the agent's observation input by changing the timing at which the action is taken. The proposed approach involves two key components: a predictor that estimates the time it takes for an action to produce a specific observation, and a timing controller that generates the optimal timing sequence. Experimental results indicate that this novel attack strategy can successfully deceive target agents with high success rates, but with minimal computational resources.

This study investigates the characteristics of in-plane magnetic fields on a two-dimensional wallpaper group P2m2m2 crystal. Calculations indicate that an in-plane magnetic field applied to this type of lattice can lead to a linear dispersion known as a Dirac cone. Within this configuration, the Dirac points exhibited stability under variations in lattice tight-binding parameters and magnetic field strength. Nevertheless, an out-of-plane magnetic field has the potential to disrupt these Dirac points, causing them to either shift or vanish. As a result, the research offers valuable insights for exploring adjustable Dirac cones in specialized magnetic environments.

A stochastic optimization method called risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RSRL) allows agents to make decisions in dynamic, uncertain environments, taking into account both their expected outcomes and levels of risk. However, RSRL models are difficult to implement in non-stationary environments, where the optimal policy can change frequently and rapidly. To overcome this challenge, we develop a new RSRL model based on a graph-based matrix factorization approach, allowing for the identification of changing patterns in flow and cost data. The model divides environmental costs into stable and volatile components and uses dynamic regret to measure its performance, achieving optimal results for RSRL by bounding regret within a logarithmic factor. The model offers two advantages: it can automatically identify when the environment changes, and it has a separate design option that allows users to set the frequency of changes themselves.

The adoption of web services in enterprises has led to a significant increase in software development projects, which in turn have been managed through project tracking tools such as Jira. This has resulted in a vast amount of data being generated about enterprise projects, primarily in the form of issue management system data (IMS D). Despite research interest in analyzing IMSD for process improvement, the data's sensitivity hinders sharing with researchers. To overcome this limitation, a collaborative effort was initiated to identify and redact potentially sensitive data. The resulting dataset comprises issues collected from 20 public Jira repositories representing 14 distinct software development processes. This dataset enables researchers to study text-based issue management data and ultimately facilitates further research into enterprise project optimization.

One of the primary obstacles in distributed machine learning is efficiently averaging model parameters. This study introduces a novel family of aggregation functions, rooted in a continuous path between Cauchy's median and arithmetic mean, to compute the average of non-negative integers. The method is both simpler and more flexible than existing approaches, while also more resistant to noise and malicious attacks. The theoretical properties of this family are analyzed and its performance in various distributed learning settings is evaluated through experiments. The results show that our aggregation functions significantly outperform alternatives in scenarios involving noise and malicious attacks.

We propose and simulate an integrated trap system using a chip-scale diffraction array to capture and hold a single ruby Raman molecule. The setup incorporates a on-chip Ramsey interferometer and all-optical manipulation and detection tools. The proposed design leverages structural light to efficiently utilize available light and maximizes the information gained from photon detection. Our findings show that this method has the potential to enhance the efficiency of single-atom detectors and improve the speed and efficiency of quantum information processing by a factor of 5 to 10 compared to conventional methods.

Let the free monoid over the alphabet $\Lambda$ in an ordered relationship be denoted as $\Lambda^{\ast}$, with its Herbrand tree $\Lambda^{\ast T}$, and its syntactic completion $\Lambda^{\ast \sigma}$. The completion $\Lambda^{\ast \sigma}$ is derived from $\Lambda^{\ast}$ by including all its left infinite $\Lambda^{\ast \sigma}$-sequences, which form a subset of the tree's node set $\Lambda^{\ast T}$. The order of this completion is defined as the least order that completes its $\Lambda^{\ast}$'s order relationship, making $\Lambda^{\ast \sigma}$ a complete order under its $\Lambda^{\ast T}$'s order completion. The paper's objective is to provide a method to compute the completion of the strictly positive elements in $\Lambda^{\ast \sigma}$, which can be done by using the completion of $\Lambda^{\ast}$ under its strictly positive order relationship and is based on the original word set $\Lambda^{\ast}$.

Traditional methods for creating a polymer from a set of atoms are limited to simple connections, like those found in water molecules. This is because these methods use basic techniques for deriving connections, which are insufficient for more complex molecules. To overcome this limitation, a new technique has been developed that employs a customized shortening method to create a polymer from a set of atoms, resulting in a molecule with the fewest possible connections, no connections with overlapping atoms, and no connections with adjacent vertices. The technique has been tested on various molecules and found to successfully create valid water molecules and other simple molecules. However, the technique has also been shown to struggle with molecules that have many possible connections, like those found in large proteins.

In the field of Model-Based Design, the process of aligning a mathematical model with observed data is known as calibration. When this process involves fitting a mathematical model to observed time-series data, it is referred to as direct transcription. This concept is illustrated through a scenario involving COVID-19 related challenges. Specifically, it demonstrates how to build a mathematical model of breathing patterns based on the sinusoidal model, utilize the fitted model to predict the breather's dynamics under dual-mask conditions, and compare these predictions to the breathing patterns of a second patient. This approach to direct transcription is showcased through the application of a mathematical model of breathing patterns, thereby highlighting its utility in exploring the breather's underlying dynamics through data from another individual.

Let $d$ be a positive integer and $f$ a rational function of degree $d+1$ over the complex numbers, which when raised to the power of two results in a critically linear function. We show that the set of functions that can be obtained by repeatedly applying $f$ and normalization forms a finite and abelian group.

For linear regression models in high-dimensional settings, this research investigates the implications of two characteristic functions, specifically designed to measure the accuracy of linear approximations, on empirical Bayes methods for estimating the unknown error variance. We consider whether certain conditions are met when many variables are included, and our analysis shows that one characteristic function can simultaneously assess the accuracy of several Bayesian estimators, such as mean absolute and squared errors. Notably, this finding enables us to establish the validity of least-squares risk reduction procedures in these complex environments.

Machine tools are expensive investments in manufacturing facilities, and their effective operation is crucial for businesses to minimize energy consumption and ensure profitability. To address the energy usage issue, our research centers around examining the power requirements of vertical machining centers to streamline energy management. A statistical method rooted in Bayesian evaluation and optimized through a genetic algorithm is utilized to accurately forecast the energy consumption of these machines. This approach integrates power data from machining operations to develop reliable regression models. The proposed technique outperforms traditional optimization methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency, and its success has been validated using real-world machining center data.

The spectral dimension of a graph is defined by the decay rate of return probabilities in a random walk on that graph. This dimension can be connected to dimensions defined within metric spaces, such as Hausdorff or Ahlfors regular conformal measures. This note considers spectral dimension as a property of an abstract graph, and when a graph's parameters satisfy certain conditions, we demonstrate the existence of a measure that is both Ahlfors regular and conformal. This generalisation of spectral dimension allows us to obtain results regarding random walks that similar to those found in existing literature, and we also determine when these dimensions are equivalent.

A new approach to determine the physical solution of the QCD wavefunction in the mass eigenstate basis is implemented by merging $\eta$ and $\eta'$ components and compared to the solution in the gluon basis. The implementation involves summing all $\eta$ and $\eta'$ state combinations with weights derived from the flavor singlet, octet, and gluon coefficients in the mass eigenstate state. Results from the $\eta$-$\eta'$ blending method show closer agreement with the experimental mass of the $\meson$ than the gluon basis method, with the former providing a significant improvement over the latter. Furthermore, the ratio of gluon contributions to the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ components indicates that gluon contributions through the $\meson$ and $\eta'$ states are in line with experimental data on the mass of the $\meson$, with a gluon fraction specifically matching experimental findings.

A comprehensive evaluation of existing signature verification templates was conducted to assess their safety and efficiency. This study thoroughly examined the distinct characteristics, level of complexity, and ability to be reproduced from a set of 300 hand-written signature templates, representing 30 individuals signing their names in a single pass. The signature collection process involved using two common input devices, the signature line and the 2D tablet, along with device-specific feature extraction techniques. For the template's uniqueness and intricacy assessment, a sliding window-based matching method was employed against non-overlapping or overlapping portions of genuine signatures. Conversely, verified copies of the signature were produced after a one-week break and processed using the same extraction methods. The results revealed that numerical values, such as the area under the curve and the Zernike moment, proved effective in verifying signatures on the signature line but were ineffective for 2D devices. On the other hand, the binned histogram feature showed superior performance and capability across all scenarios and devices. Furthermore, it was observed that some enrolled individuals exhibited higher complexity and uniqueness in their signatures compared to others, and this was consistent across all devices.

We investigate the four-derivative type II non-supersymmetric vacua derived from asymmetric orbifolds with the N=6 internal supersymmetry. Our analysis encompasses the cases of T^4/ (Z2 + Z2) and T^6/Z3 baselines, and we determine whether the Lorentz invariance can be preserved in the non-supersymmetric vacua by adding four-derivative correction terms. We examine the corrections in relation to the K2Z2 and K3Z3 baselines, as well as the O6-6-6 and K6 baselines. Furthermore, we explore whether the corrections in these vacua can be mapped to those in their respective supersymmetric counterparts, such as T^4/ Z2 supersymmetric and Calabi-Yau threefold baselines.

Our investigation of the equilibrium states of a lattice of spin-vortex molecules reveals, through higher-order multilinear coupling, an effective interaction of an n-th order between them, analogous to a charge of an n-th elementary unit. This effective interaction arises from the interaction between magnetic fields and views magnetic multipoles, such as spin currents, as distinct elementary components, akin to electric multipoles. The effective interaction is demonstrated to be equivalent to a spin texture with an arbitrary higher-order multipole, such as an octupole, and is observed to be analogous to a charge of an (n-1)-th elementary unit.

Two key processes, related to the formation of elements in the universe, set clear boundaries on how much $^{15}$N and $^{14}$N can be created, particularly in terms of their ratio and total amount. These constraints arise from the limited availability of $^{14}$O and the inability to produce a specific isotope ratio that matches current observations. As a direct consequence, any process that creates the various chemical forms of these elements, including the different levels of $^{15}$N found in the atmosphere and other areas, and the total amount of these elements, must be accurately reflected in the large database of nitrogen's stable isotope composition. Furthermore, this limitation also applies to the same ratios and total amounts of the corresponding oxygen isotopes.

Multilingual users are becoming increasingly common in the digital world, but research on code-mixing and switching remains limited compared to monolingual studies. Despite the growing prevalence of multilingual communities, NLP research still falls short in addressing their needs. This paper gathers the insights of various researchers and practitioners to explore the potential of N for Multilingual Communities. It begins by defining key code-mixing concepts, then examines the data availability, annotation, models, and evaluations needed to support effective MLC NLP. The paper also highlights potential research paths and hurdles to be overcome to advance MLC NLP.

Biomedical graph modeling has emerged as a prominent approach for tackling complex challenges in clinical, genetic, and basic science areas, thanks to its ability to capture relationships and patterns in heterogeneous data. This course will explore graph learning methodologies from both theoretical and practical standpoints, emphasizing recent advancements in graph neural networks and attention-based models. Furthermore, it will apply these techniques to real-world problems in disease diagnosis, prognosis, and basic science research, addressing sequence, document, and multi-modal data while considering both transductive and inductive learning settings.

Dark matter's nature remains one of physics' most intriguing aspects, with diverse models proposed to describe its possible forms, such as supersymmetry, left-right symmetric models, and multiple dark sectors. Direct detection experiments, particularly enhanced underground ones, have been instrumental in investigating these possibilities, with notable findings from experiments like the Magor Enhanced White Dwarf (MWD) experiment. This investigation examines the potential of the MWD's novel technique to set stricter constraints on the inelastic dark matter model, with a focus on its ability to detect inelastic scattering off hydrogen. Assuming suitable couplings, the MWD could achieve this within three to four orders of magnitude. Furthermore, the MWD's sensitivity in detecting inelastic scattering off helium could significantly surpass existing bounds from the Fermi-LAT and Fermi-LSS experiments, particularly for dark matter masses under ten MeV. Similarly, the MWD's bounds on supersymmetric models, specifically coannihilation with stop and chargino states, surpass the existing limits from the Large Hadron Collider and the CMB experiments. Notably, the MWD's limits on unsplit doublets in these models exceed the limits from the Fermi-LSS. Finally, the MWD's detection of inelastic scattering off neon and other elements could significantly surpass the limits from the Fermi-LSS.

Advancements in deep learning have led to the creation of graph neural networks, which outperform other models for certain tasks, particularly in preserving confidentiality. Despite their effectiveness, existing GNN privacy methods fall short in addressing the unique requirements of graph data, leading to subpar privacy guarantees. In response, we have developed a graph privacy consultant that leverages visual information to identify and prioritize sensitive nodes and edges, enabling a more targeted approach to privacy protection. By assigning each node and edge a content-based importance score, we allow users to choose the level of privacy based on their desired balance of utility and confidentiality. Furthermore, we incorporate these scores into existing GNN private training methods to further optimize the privacy-utility trade-off. Experimental results demonstrate that our graph privacy consultant outperforms current methods, producing more accurate predictions while enhancing confidentiality.

This paper explores four theoretical models of a hidden market segmentation, where some consumers only purchase products that are explicitly labeled as environmentally friendly. It examines the impact of this segmentation on product disclosure decisions, assuming that producers have varying levels of knowledge about the true environmental value of their products. In situations where products have the same potential to be environmentally friendly, if there is any doubt about their environmental impact, the product will not be disclosed and instead, it will be assumed to have no environmental impact. Conversely, if the environmental impact of an unpurchased product is known to be substantial, the product will be disclosed even if its environmental performance is not certain. Furthermore, if environmentally friendly products tend to be larger in size, they are more likely to be disclosed assuming that there is any chance they could be better than neutral. Lastly, if the environmental impact varies independently of production costs, then lower-priced products are more likely to be disclosed.

This study compares the fragmentation patterns of light-quark and gluon jets within proton-proton and aluminum lead collisions. By employing JETCLF taggers, we identify quark and gluon jets in the ATLAS detector at the CERN LHC, analyzing $pp$ collisions at 7 TeV and aluminum lead collisions at 5.02 TeV with a total transverse energy of 4.07 PeV. Utilowing simulation data, we isolate gluon jets in the $pp$ sample, whereas light-quark jets are selected in aluminum lead samples. Key fragmentation parameters, including the cumulative fragmentation function, spray shape, and broadening, are examined. Comparing aluminum lead and gluon jet fragments, we observe the medium-induced radiation effect in gluon jets, which exhibits a noticeable alteration in the cumulative fragmentation function, spray shape, and light-quark jet-like broadening within a 30-degree cone.

The CP2K program package, which handles atomistic simulations by integrating molecular dynamics and electronic structure theory, has been widely adopted in scientific research. Recent developments in the package have spanned electronic structure theory, maxwell equations, and fast force calculation methods. Although recent versions have been successful, particularly the 3.0 release, further improvements are being pursued to enhance performance, such as scaling to larger systems, executing on larger computing clusters, and extending its applicability to newer hardware. As we approach exascale computing, it is crucial to explore new possibilities and strategies to maintain and improve the package's existing high performance.

Coronal solar plasma can emit hard X-rays when nonthermal electrons are accelerated and accelerated against active regions of the corona. The intensity of these emitted rays serves as a measure of the product of the accelerated electron population and their average energy. Observations from the Focus Optical Spectrograph for Imaging (FOXSI) on the Big Bear Solar Telescope reveal that there are very faint HXR sources on the solar surface, linked to bright holes in the radio spectrum. Despite initially meeting the criteria for a HXR emission, further investigation shows that these faint signals fall below the reliability threshold for a genuine HXR emission, likely linked to the detection threshold of FOXSI. As such, they could be useful in understanding the coronal solar plasma and its HXR emission characteristics, given improved detection capabilities.

Predicting social impact from visual content is a task made more complex by the presence of various forms of social bias. Traditional machine learning models can be trained with limited data, but to avoid inheriting social biases, they require extensive and carefully curated datasets. Recent research has shown that certain neural network architectures, such as graph neural networks (GNNs), excel in social impact prediction. However, standard RNN-based duration augmentation methods do not take into consideration the inherent characteristics of GNNs. In order to address this discrepancy, we have developed a socially biased social impact prediction system that is enhanced by user reviews, and further improved by two innovative duration augmentation techniques - a social duration augmentation-RNN and a user duration augmentation-RNN - both of which are tailored to the properties of GNNs. These enhanced models outperform existing RNN and GNN augmentation methods on social impact prediction, as demonstrated by our experimental results.

The dimension of the phase space in Euler-Arnold equations on a Lie algebra directly correlates with the putative central charge of a conformal field theory (CFT) made up of free fields. In our study, we establish an association between a specific type of conformal field theory, derived from Euler-Arnold equations on a Lie algebra, with CFTs described by Dirac brackets. This relationship is exemplified by Shapere-Taylor's phase space CFT, showing it to be equivalent to a free boson theory, and also drawing a connection to conformal field theories related to Drinfel'd-Sokolov hierarchy, which and also free boson on a circle after free fermions on a circle after obtaining a Lagrangian submanifold.

All-in-all, the Complete Least Squares estimator offers the most reliable position estimation method to date, yet it suffers from being computationally expensive and difficult to implement due to its need for a complete and precise system map. To address these limitations, the present study proposes two alternative strategies to position determination based on the Incomplete Least Squares principle. The first strategy involves iteratively refining the map via the EM algorithm until the resulting ILS solution is sufficient for the desired accuracy. The second strategy utilizes multiple map variants and selects the one producing the least discrepancy in final results. Both strategies demonstrate improved efficiency over their previous iterations and are validated as providing optimal outcomes. Furthermore, the present work introduces a new criterion to evaluate the reliability of final positions. The proposed method's efficacy is confirmed through computer simulations and a real-world wireless localization system implementation.

Researchers investigating the early universe often explore the possibility of hidden sectors, which could have formed separate temperatures due to limited interaction with normal matter.  A key question is how the various temperatures would equalize.  A new model proposes that a heavy particle, acting as a thermal connector, interacts with both the visible and hidden matter.  Using an example with neutrinophiles neutrons as the primary thermal bridge to neutrinos, calculations show that neutrons can effectively transfer energy even at low velocities.  This indicates that neutrons could have played a crucial role in establishing a single temperature for the entire universe before rapidly disappearing.

A comprehensive search for same-sign W boson pairs generated by forces other than weak interaction has been conducted using proton-proton collision data at 13 TeV, recorded by the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. The analysis, which involves approximately 27 million proton-proton collisions, focuses on events containing two same-sign charged leptons and at least two jets. The events are categorized by event characteristics, and upper production rate limits are established at a 95% confidence level, ranging from 0.20 to 24 picobombs, dependent on dilepton invariant mass and jet activity. The most stringent rate is found to be 0.20 picobombs for events with low invariant mass and significant jet activity. These limits are applied to four theories predicting new particles mediating the process, and the predicted event occurrences are generally below the predicted values for predicted new particle parameters.

A significant obstacle in developing robust color adaptation techniques for video is the issue of domain gaps between images captured by different cameras due to color variations. This problem has limited existing methods that are designed for within-camera variations. This research tackles the cross-camera color adaptation challenge for video, covering both real-world and synthetic images. We developed a new approach called cross-camera deep tinting (C-DT), which aligns the RGB image distributions across different color spaces by matching their first and second moments. The proposed method constructs a linear transformation matrix in the RGB domain, eliminating the need for complex generative models. The proposed C-DT method is versatile and can be applied to various vision tasks, including novel view synthesis, radiance field interpolation, and image-based rendering. C-DT has achieved remarkable results on video color adaptation, outperforming other approaches in terms of visual quality and efficiency.

A method to compare any two datasets without assuming a specific cosmological model is developed, and then applied to examine potential deviations from flatness in the $\Lambda$CDM cosmology. By treating curvature as the only variable of interest and models with zero curvature as the baseline, a new statistical test is devised. This test, along with similar tests for other cosmological parameters, allows us to determine whether this parameter estimation method yields results comparable to those from standard parameter estimation. When applied to four distinct cosmological datasets, and including simulations with up to 10 times more noise than the actual data, the four datasets consistently find that they are compatible with curved spacetime, and also find that the bent models are favored over the flat ones, with preferences ranging from an Akaike weights of 0.75 to 0.95 in favor of the bent models. However, standard parameter estimation methods result in models with Akaike weights of 0.9999 in favor of the flat models, and yield results that are significantly more precise than those from the four datasets. These findings illustrate that comparing datasets with curvature estimates obtained through a model-independent approach can yield significantly different results from those obtained through standard parameter estimation methods, and that curvature estimates obtained through this alternative method favor values that are slightly different from zero, and significantly more than the zero values obtained through standard estimation methods.

The internet has become a vast repository for information, with a significant portion consisting of redundant or deteriorated content.  While traditional web maintenance, aimed at synchronizing mirrors and archives, has been extensively studied, it's now evident that's not the only form of web maintenance needed.  With a shift in focus to the web of data, particularly software, it's becoming apparent that maintaining existing content can be equally, if not more, important.  This article delves into a novel category of web maintenance: meta-maintenance, encompassing actions like updating outdated content and modifying content for security reasons.  Using meta-maintenance as a lens, we investigate changes to identical files on GitHub, a popular software development platform.  By analyzing a sample of 25,000 files and their modifications over time, we identify various triggers for these modifications and the benefits associated with them, ultimately uncovering a hidden layer of web maintenance that's often overlooked.

BD And is an eclipsing binary star system that presents characteristics of both BD Andromedae and Gamma Doradus type stars. By analyzing light curves created through space-based photometry, precise orbital and physical parameters of this system were determined. The resulting mean radial velocities for BD And A and B stars are -10.7 km/s and -12.1 km/s respectively. The masses for BD And A and B stars are 1.27 M and 1.12 M, and the stellar radii are 1.25 R and 1.20 R. The stellar surface temperatures are 7176 K and 7030 K. The mass values align with expectations, but the stellar radius and corresponding pulsation period are larger than expected, indicating BD And may resemble a BD Andromedae star.

This article builds upon a previous study by the author and Struwe, extending their results by considering a more broad range of data for the fractional Yamabe flow. It builds upon a method introduced by Munteanu and the author for solving the equation.

Cross-domain recommendation has gained significant attention in recent years by combining recommendation data from multiple domains to boost sparse coverage and enhance collaborative filtering across various domains. Current approaches typically learn domain-independent preferences based on common user-item interactions and independent latent factors, but recent research has demonstrated that comprehensive preference learning can lead to superior collaboration and cross-domain recommendations. Building upon these findings, our study introduces a new method called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR), which promotes collaborative filtering in multiple sparse domains through enhanced comprehensive preference learning. Specifically, MSDCR integrates both shared and domain-specific user preferences and item attributes in a unified latent space and employs a multi-sparse-domain cooperative strategy to improve inter-domain cooperation and cross-domain recommendations. An innovative inter-domain linkage strategy is introduced in MSDCR to increase the connectivity between different domains and leverage more effective collaborative filtering methods. Our inter-domain linkage strategy aims to maximize the sharing of common preferences between domains and minimize domain-specific preferences. Experimental results on real-world datasets have demonstrated that MSDCR consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art recommendation methods in terms of accuracy, robustness, and efficiency for cross-domain and multi-sparse-domain cooperative recommendations.

We establish deformation theories for perpendicular and symplectic bundle morphism compositions that are orthogonal and unitary respectively, and demonstrate how these theories relate to the deformation theory of perpendicular and symplectic matrices.

Let P_{<k}(x) = \sum a_r \frac{x^r}{r!} be a polynomial where a_r represents the count of partitions of a set with r elements, each having less than k distinct parts. The study reveals the multiplicative relationship between the generating functions P_{<2}(x), P_{<3}(x), and P_{<4}(x), demonstrating that for each relationship, there exists a multiplicative structure. The results reveal the underlying multiplicative nature of these partition functions with constraints of less than k distinct parts.

This research focuses on the robustness of common error models for least squares estimation, particularly in noisy environments. To this end, we examine the relative robustness of the standard L2 estimation method in relation to alternative models, such as L1 estimation and median-based methods, for determining linear relationships between two variables. We also investigate how different estimation methods can help recover true linear relationships from various types of corrupted data, including uniform noise, parabolic distortion, and other types of outliers.

This study investigates the production distribution of J/ψ, ψ(2S), X(3872) and Bc in proton-proton collisions, utilizing proton lead and nucleus nucleus collisions at various energies. Our analysis focuses on proton lead and LHCb data from nucleus nucleus collisions. We examine the nuclear modification factor and compare it to predictions from color glass condensate and perturbative QCD models. Additionally, we investigate cold and cold-like nuclear matter effects on the production of X(3872) and make recommendations for further research on this enigmatic particle. Our work also considers how J/ψ feed-down data may impact our understanding of Bc dissimilarities in nucleus nucleus collisions.

Within the Hubbard model, disorder is introduced into the chain, with the disorder strength controlled by the ratio of disorder to inter-electron interaction.  Numerical findings using level statistics and transmission spectra suggest the emergence of singular phases, with a transition between these phases occurring at the aforementioned ratio of approximately 2.  9 times the interaction.  Near this threshold, singular characteristics appear, with the length of interconnected electron segments increasing without bound.  This observation aligns with previous work on disorder-free electron-interlectron interaction systems.  Moreover, the singular phases map onto analogous models without disorder.

Our study is a direct extension of an earlier proof by Regev and Stasinski for the A-type, focusing on the fundamental group of the finite Coxeter complex for Coxeter groups of the A_n, B_n, and D_n series.

In recent years, there has been significant interest in scalar field theories that incorporate a scalar multiplet with an $SU(2)$ in symmetry, as suggested by GUT models and dark energy theories. However, the study of solitons in such theories is complicated due to the constraint that total charge must be conserved, leading many researchers to turn their attention to scalar fields with $SO(2)$ in symmetry. We develop a general framework for two-dimensional scalar field theories that incorporate a potential with no symmetry but do maintain $SO(2)$ in symmetry. Our analysis reveals that non-trivial solitons can emerge when the number of scalar fields is odd and there are no monotonic potentials. Additionally, we propose various potential models and simulate some of them to simulate soliton collisions.

We introduce a novel Bayesian framework that enables agents to learn optimal policies through inverse reinforcement learning, even when observing regulated agents who selectively execute actions based on their underlying optimal policy, while potentially using other actions as mistakes. Existing methods for inverse RL struggle to effectively tackle this scenario. Our proposed framework decomposes the inference of the teacher's optimal reward function into two distinct hierarchical learning components. Furthermore, this framework has a beneficial side effect, allowing us to accurately infer the regulating factor and the error-prone rate, two crucial yet unobservable characteristics. These attributes can then be utilized to enhance the robustness of the learned teacher reward function against variations in data. Through comprehensive numerical experiments, our framework demonstrates superior performance compared to several relevant benchmarks.

The coverage of loop transfer regions in literature spans various subsets of the fundamental group's fundamental domain, yet its full characterization remains undefined. C. Hsu and D. J. N. Limebeer proposed an approach to assess small loop transfer regions but restricted it to the set of Hermitian matrices, $\mathbb{H}_+^{n\times n}$. This research introduces a more general concept, known as a robust small loop transfer region, applicable to specific subgroups of the fundamental group, specifically those involving automorphisms of Hermitian matrices, $\mathbb{H}_{\pm}^{n\times n}$. Characterization of these regions is provided through two distinct methods: one based on a convex optimization approach and the other utilizing Lagrange multipliers. The proposed methods are validated with numerical examples.

A new approach to resolving complex control problems, which traditional reinforcement learning (RL) finds challenging, has been developed. This method leverages the capabilities of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to learn a policy directly through trial and error. The proposed solution involves a two-step process: initially, DRL is used to acquire a rough control strategy, and then this strategy is refined by mapping it to a more effective policy for the original problem. This strategy is demonstrated to successfully resolve a range of control problems that have proven difficult for both classical RL and other methods. The primary contribution of this research is the introduction of this two-staged DRL method, offering a novel approach to addressing this longstanding control issue.

This study examines the growth of supermassive black holes over 12 billion years by comparing observed mass distributions to those predicted by simulations. It specifically focuses on supermassive black holes that form early on, more than a billion years after the Big Bang. By matching the predicted mass distributions from simulations to those observed in the Chandra Deep Field South and the HF2-2 fields, the research provides constraints on the properties of their host black holes. Results indicate that early supermassive black holes likely formed from massive seeds weighing thousands of times that of the sun. However, by looking at later supermassive black holes in clusters and comparing them to those that formed early on, the research suggests that many of these early, heavy black holes may have grown through accretion of surrounding gas rather than through merging with other black holes. This could be because massive black holes form early on in environments with plenty of available matter.

Recent advancements in inelastic neutron scattering and associated computational techniques have made it possible to obtain detailed dynamic information about materials. However, the technical nature of this data and analysis methods has caused it to remain isolated from other chemical and solid state characterization techniques. To achieve this goal, we have created open-source software that links experimental data with multiple theoretical models in an intuitive way. By doing so, we provide not only convenient access to this information, but also detailed insights into the network's predictions, allowing for deeper analysis and learning.

In the past thirty years, the foundation of the internet enabled a global community of researchers to gather and share new scientific discoveries before formal publication in a publication. This prepublication activity began as a small community, driven by researchers' desire to cite and track the work of others, and quickly grew into a global practice. This present study reviews the history and development of prepublication services, examining key milestones and decisions that shaped the community and its platform services. Through this historical perspective, the analysis seeks to identify ongoing challenges and potential future trends in prepublication activities.

Digital recording and analysis of experimental data play a crucial role in scientific research, specifically in physical sciences. Traditional lab notebooks have specific limitations such as character restrictions, which the Digital Lab Journal app overcomes by providing an interface for creating and managing digital records of experiments. This journal app functionality allows users to create and organize custom entities and properties, which can then be used to record experiment data in an organized and customizable format. Furthermore, the digital journal can export its content in various formats, including CSV and JSON, which can then be combined and analyzed using data visualization and management tools.

High-entropy alloys, which consist of multiple principal elements, exhibit exceptional mechanical, chemical, and physical properties. Despite these advantages, their complex nature poses significant challenges in identifying suitable compositions due to the vast number of potential combinations. To overcome this obstacle, machine learning has emerged as a powerful tool to rapidly and efficiently explore the compositional design space. This review summarizes the recent advancements in applying machine learning to high-entropy alloy design, highlighting existing challenges and potential opportunities, as well as future directions.

We examine a hypothetical partner of the $T_{cc}^+$ diquark-exchanged diquark-antidiquark state, specifically the $T_{cc}^+D^{\ast+}D^0$ or $T_{cc}^+D^{\ast0}D^+$ system, that decays into a $D^{\ast}D\pi$ final state via the $T_{cc}^+$ dissociation. This study investigates possible reactions which can lead to such a $D^{\ast}D\pi$ state, specifically the $D^{\ast+}D^-\pi^+$, $D^{\ast+}D\pi^0$, and $D^{\ast0}D^+$ processes. Utilizing the light-front Bethe-Salpeter equation, we calculate the transition amplitude for these reactions and determine a transition form factor, finding that the calculated form factor is consistent with experimental measurements from the LHCb collaboration.

Machine learning models based on ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and stochastic differential equations (SDEs) can effectively capture complex, noisy data. However ODEs and SDEs struggle to explain observations made from real-world data because they cannot directly model the underlying patterns in the data. Graph neural networks provide a framework for learning from both local and global aspects of the data, but they are not well-suited for representing the temporal dynamics in the data. There is a pressing need for a novel model that combines the capabilities of ODEs, SDEs, graph neural networks and latent variable learning to better understand the hidden dynamics in the data. We introduce a new graph ODE/ SDE model that uses latent variables and leverages the time-series capabilities of ODEs/ SDEs and the temporal and diffusion properties of ODEs/ SDEs and graph neural networks to better model the time-dependent dynamics in the data. The proposed model has been tested on synthetic data and real-life cardiac OEC datasets, and the results show that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, including cardiac OEC datasets, in terms of predictive performance and interpretability.

The lowest possible upper limit of the degree of a vector-valued function of n binary variables with a maximum distance of $\delta$ from linearity is determined by second degree functions, where it is set to $2^{\ell-1}-2$. It is known that to achieve this bound, specific subsets of the variables must meet certain criteria, and it is found that these subsets must be a certain type of set, and it is known that for a set to meet these criteria, it must have a minimum size, and it is found that a set of a certain type can be found with a minimum size, and it is found that the size of these sets can be found to be at least a certain value, and it is found that the size of these sets can be found to be at most a certain value, and it is found that the size of these sets can be found to be at least a certain value times the logarithm of the set size, and it is found that the size of these sets can be found to be at most a certain value times the square of the set size, and it is found that the size of these sets can be found to be at least a certain value, and it is found that the size of these sets can be found to be at most a certain value, and it is found that the size of these sets can be found to be at least a certain value, and it is found that the size of these sets can be found to

Binarized neural networks offer improved inference speed and data storage efficiency at the expense of training complexity. We present a novel non-negative non-convex optimization problem for binairezation that allows for exact recovery of the original pre-softmax matrix. To address precision constraints, we propose a fixed margin constraint and develop an alternating optimization algorithm alternating between the original matrix and its binarized counterpart. The original matrix is updated using the projected subgradient algorithm and the matrix quantization step is simplified to only sign quantization. The original matrix and the quantized matrix are then exactly reconstructed from one another. The original training approach is extended to support asymmetric fixed margin cross-entropy loss and non-uniform sampling of binarized matrices. The original loss and sampling approach are equivalent to the margin-cross-entropy loss and binarized cross-entropy loss of the original matrix, respectively. The original approach and its extensions are demonstrated on the binaryized deep neural networks and achieve comparable performance to their non-binarized counterparts.

The publication "Theoretical Framework for PDF Fitting" proposes a formal foundation for parton distribution function descriptions and their subsequent evaluation, incorporating latest QCD predictive models and advanced fitting techniques, including Bayesian methods.

This document highlights the capabilities of the ELKI algorithm, a versatile tool 
for clustering and dimensionality reduction, in various applications. It serves 
as both a comprehensive, easy-to-use API and a straightforward collection of 
algorithm implementations, making it user-friendly for integration into high-level 
applications and integration of new algorithms. It also provides essential testing 
frameworks to ensure reliable results. Written in Java, the algorithm library can 
be effortlessly combined due to its properties. It is presented as a valuable 
resource and element of the ELKI project, along with details on the development 
team and its connection to the University of Heidelberg.

A new technique has been created to quickly create an optical frequency comb using microresonators by leveraging the effects of optical solitons and microcomb generation. This approach enables the rapid formation of the comb, with a single sweep taking less than 10 milliseconds. In contrast, traditional methods can take as long as 10 seconds. The new technique involves simultaneously applying pumps at the "resonator breakdown" threshold while using a blue-detuned modulation to create the comb. This technique allows for the creation of the entire comb or individual lines at any desired wavelength by adjusting the pump power. Additionally, a demonstration of the approach has created an optical frequency grid with over 600 resolvable features, with over 100 of these features clearly visible in a 3D reconstruction of a 3D hologram.

We establish the existence of precisely two distinct, faithful, and symmetrically invariant random subgroups for any hyperbolic group that is not virtually cyclic, an finding that directly follows from their stochastic stability and origin in respectively, axial subgroups for quasi-geodesic lines and action on a hyperbolic space.

This study delves into the neural network's kernel to understand generalization in the native basis of binary weights. It presents an approximate kernel formula based on Legendre polynomials, providing an analytical tool to investigate the behavior of binary weight networks. Through empirical tests, the study validates this approximation and examines its implications for understanding and further reduction of binary weight networks. Notably, the study discovers that lower quantization levels lead to better generalization, and certain conditions under which exact equivalence between quantized networks and their floating-point counterparts can be achieved.

A generalized entropy functional is created for p = 1 and p > 1 quantum critical surfaces within asymptotically anti-de Sitter spacetimes, extending the concept of entropy into higher-dimensional boundaries. It's demonstrated that these entropies satisfy the strong subadditivity principle and are represented by a set of inequalities known as the hologentropy inequality, generalizing Jackiewicz and Lashkevich's results. Additionally, calculating the surface for a Pomenansky-Liebschetz entanglement region in a four-dimensional asymptotically anti-de Sitter black hole results in a complex expression that requires numerical methods for solution, which is then illustrated in terms of radius and thermal R-charge for certain cases and compared with previous theories.

The intersection multiplier is a key measurement for the efficiency of Barnes-Hut type methods, enabling an assessment of how much more expensive model calculation is compared to individual object evaluation. In this study, the intersection multiplier for solvable lattice frameworks is determined, with general findings applied to two particular cases: the gravitational N-body problem and simulating particle interactions within molecular systems using van der Waals or Coulomb forces. It's discovered that, for particles arranged in specific patterns, the calculation cost drops significantly, particularly in grids designed to minimize overlap between bounding boxes and particles. This occurs when the covering factor of such frameworks equals one, a condition that can be achieved through a specific adjustment of control parameters.

A common approach in solving underdetermined linear systems is the Iterative Thresholding algorithm, which has multiple variants. We analyze a modified version of this algorithm, incorporating stabilization, and show that it outperforms its unsimplified counterparts. Moreover, we establish both the convergence and error bounds of this algorithm and have also tested it experimentally on numerical examples.

We examined the image brightness fluctuations within bright and extended objects like the Orion Nebula and Cassiopeia A. The fluctuations were quantified using power spectra, both total and polarized, which we compared to the power spectra of individual images from a line integral camera (LIC) observing Orion Nebula and the Chandra X-ray telescope observing Cassiopeia A. The comparisons revealed that the power spectra of combined images represent those of individual images, a finding that validates their use for measuring polarized emission ratios and determining the 3D structure of Orion Nebula and the afterglow of Cassiopeia A. Our research also provided estimates of spatial resolution for LIC and Chandra images, effectively broadening the applicable spatial frequency range of their spatial frequency measurements.

We introduce new probabilistic models, the "SLE-log-gas model" and the "SLE-CKG model," for Gaussian free fields on an infinite plane or a bounded region with Dirichlet boundary conditions. The models originate from Peisson subcritical SLE cliques, first proposed by Sheffer. On the infinite plane, the model is defined through the joint distribution of chordal SLEs and Carleman-Ahlfors coordinates of Sheffer cliques, with the SLEs representing a holomorphic function's boundary mappings, and the Carleman-Ahlford maps from the unit disk. On bounded domains with Dirichlet boundary conditions, the model arises from conditioning on Brownian motion values. Both models can be understood as a coupling of SLEs and CGFs, with the conditioning on CGFs' values at specific points resulting in zero at those points.
