The influence of heat on dissipation is comparable to that of active alcohol
dissipation, occurring through enhanced dissipation in a specific viscosity range.
In this range, heat generates additional energy and changes the way it's dissipated,
ultimately leading to increased dissipation rates. This phenomenon was observed
across different types of turbulent flows and is independent of the type of fluid
used to simulate the heat.

A new class of magnetic semiconductors known as geometric magnetoelectrics features unique magnetoelectric properties driven by topological properties. The defining characteristics of this group of materials are its magnetoelectric response, which is both linear and quadratic in nature. The strength of the underlying geometric or topological class determines the magnitude of the linear and quadratic responses. The study of models representing this class has revealed additional non-linear responses beyond the initially identified ones. The most significant of these additional responses is found in three-dimensional topological insulators with a gap and time-reversal symmetry. These models exhibit chiral Witten effects and other properties. The primary characteristics of this group of materials are explained and derived from a non-Abelian geometric response theory. The theory also enables the calculation of geometric contributions to transport coefficients and topological invariants. The invariants can be experimentally measured when the materials are doped with magnetic impurities, which change their topological class and cause geometric Hall conductivities with invariants that are half-integer values.

In various fields, linear chaos exhibits notable characteristics. This letter delves into the study of linear systems with delayed feedback, where the time lag plays a crucial role in feedback. It's found that varying the time lag can greatly amplify dispersion in phase space, where even a slight perturbation can lead to significant divergent trajectories over time. The research reveals that the system's time lag must be precisely tuned to achieve maximum dispersion amplification, where the time it takes for trajectories to separate by a factor of 10 can be reduced by over a thousand times. The findings also reveal that the system displays nonlinearity-like dispersion patterns, where the rate of trajectory separation varies depending on the specific values of system parameters. The maximum dispersion amplification occurs at specific values of parameters and happens when the delayed signal in the system is out of phase with the current state, where removing the time lag modulation leads to completely different behavior.

This study builds on previous work to investigate D-continuations, which serve as a precise, probabilistic form of semantic model for lambda calculus. It extends these concepts to cover all lambda terms, ensuring that semantic values are consistently defined within specific types, regardless of convergence. By integrating the newly developed semantics with global semantics, which also ensure consistent semantic values, this research proves that both semantics model congruence for all lambda terms and exhibit exponential almost-sure equivalence.

A new challenge is introduced to the field of NLP, which involves the 'Design Dialogue Mining' task. This involves extracting meaningful dialogues from a domain-specific text that reflects the evolution of a product design. To overcome the limitations of traditional dialogue mining methods, a new framework is presented that focuses on mining design dialogues from NLP text. This framework utilizes a data-driven approach to identify and analyze the underlying design processes and outcomes, thereby providing a new perspective on the application of NLP in design research.

A proposed solution to the hierarchy and strong CP problems involves the macro-quantum-coherent field resulting from the Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking of the Standard Model's SU(2)xU(1) gauge fields, typically described as Goldstone bosons and a Higgs field. This time-like field, which we suggest emerges from a post-inflation quantum vacuum fluctuation, forms the basis of the long-range gravity we experience, with its coherent mass distribution giving rise to the Curvature Tensor through Einstein's Field Equations. Furthermore, we propose that this field's Cauchy problem, involving Cauchy-Riemann equations, may provide a basis for the Cauchy-Kowalewski initial value problem for General Relativity, with its cause-effect relationship being retro-causal, as indicated by its negative U(1) phase, and its U(1) symmetry representing the conservation of mass-energy, with its mass being the source of the Cauchy curvature.

Proximal methods, such as the Moreau-Yosida regularization, transform difficult optimization issues on complex manifolds into simpler problems on flat planes, making them easier to solve. This paper shows that when these manifold-identified optimization problems have a unique global minimum, the manifold-identified optimization problem is well-behaved and its difficult sub-problem has a unique global minimum as the penalty parameter approaches zero. Consequently, the manifold-identified optimization problem can be solved using trusted software, which often utilizes Newton methods. Moreover, the paper proves the Newton method's speed of convergence for solving this sub-problem under specific conditions. A pre-conditioned version of this sub-problem is also considered, which improves computational efficiency by reducing complex matrix operations to vector operations. This paper illustrates the method's effectiveness on two manifolds: finding rotations and shapes of quadrupeds.

In a commutative ring, a proper ideal $I$ is considered weakly $1$-prime if the product of any two elements in the ring either belongs to $I$ or their sum and the ideal are contained within $I$. Building upon this concept, the paper extends the idea of weakly $1$-prime ideals to noncommutative rings by introducing the concepts of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals and strongly weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals. These new ideals satisfy a specific condition: for any three elements $a, b, c$ in the ring, the product of the ideals generated by these elements either belongs to $I$ or its elements are contained within $I$. The paper then examines key properties and establishes relationships between feebly $1$-prime ideals of commutative rings and absopbing prime ideals of commutative rings.

We have successfully reconstructed 2333 B to rho minus, no, and positon neutrals, 262 B to rho plus, no, and neutrals, and 10342 B to rho zero, minus, and neutrals decays, utilizing the full data set collected by the Belle II detector between 2018 and 23. The unique feature of our method is its reliance on the charged decay products of the baryon decay, allowing for minimal background, and thus, no additional selection criteria are required. The measured branching fractions are:  7.022e-5, 7.047e-6, and 4.134e-4 respectively, with statistical uncertainties of +/- 1.53e-5, +/- 7.0e-6, and +/- 1.3e-5, as well as systematic uncertainties of +/- 1.45e-5, +/- 7.0e-6, and +/- 1.3e-5. These results are consistent with previous world records.

As stellar population synthesis matures, the spectral fitting of galaxies becomes a reliable tool for extracting population-related information. This research explores the application of spectro-photometry and a novel photonic device, known as photonic spectrometers, which utilize discrete slits to sample a galaxy's light. The synthetic spectra produced by these instruments can be compared with traditional spectra, and the spectral fits indicate that including photonic data improves the accuracy of synthetic chi-squared ($\chi^2_{\rm syn}$) by up to a factor of 10 for certain bands. The effects of slits with different widths, shapes, and a finite signal-to-noise ratio are investigated, revealing that some features are robust to noise but sensitive to slit width, while others are robust but width-sensitive. The results suggest that synthetic $\chi^2$ values serve as reliable tracers for specific parameters, and these findings provide a framework for developing new photonic instruments to determine the properties of galaxies.

Predicting the compatibility of medication pairs is a critical task in medicine. A deep learning model has been designed to learn from an graph of medications, capturing their characteristics and interactions for a more accurate assessment of drug pairs. This model's relational features can also be applied to other types of drug guidance problems.

Maintaining the condition of roads is a critical responsibility for transportation agencies, involving regular inspections to detect any deteriorating road sections and prioritizing necessary repairs. Traditionally, this process relies on specialized vehicles equipped with sensors to analyze road conditions. However, these vehicles are costly to maintain, making it difficult for smaller transportation departments to afford them. An alternative approach utilizes smartphone technology, taking advantage of a large database of previously collected data to train a machine learning model that can identify road irregularities without ongoing data collection costs. This study presents a method that leverages a pre-trained model, which was initially developed using data from the US, to detect road irregularities in Thailand, demonstrating that a extensively trained model can effectively recognize road irregularities across different countries, even without country-specific training.

Many creatures acquire new skills by watching others and replicating their actions.
However, simply observing someone performing a task isn't enough to understand how to do it yourself because what you see doesn't represent the action in the same way images or videos do.
Current techniques for learning from others struggle when trying to transfer skills between very different environments because they can only understand observations, not the underlying actions.
To overcome this challenge, our approach involves teaching robots to imitate the effects of actions by observing them in multiple types of situations.
This allows them to start mastering basic movements and eventually tackle complex tasks in their own unique environments.
To achieve this, our strategy involves learning a versatile representation of actions that can be used to predict the changes in the environment caused by those actions.
This action representation is organized into distinct movements, which our system learns to mimic by watching others do them in various settings.
This technique allows for new and adaptable skills to be created by combining these basic movements.
We tested our approach on simple and complex tasks that involve both two and three-dimensional environments and observed successful transfers of skills between observations that are very different in appearance.

In the context of Population III protostars, we examine the impact of a rapidly increasing magnetic field on the formation of disks. Utilizing two-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations, we observe that a magnetic field growth rate exceeding a certain threshold, specifically the epicyclic frequency, eradicates disk fragmentation. Furthermore, we discover that a magnetic field with a winding number greater than approximately 0.5 effectively inhibits the gravitational wave instability. We model the magnetic field's behavior using an analytical approach and incorporate our simulation findings into analytical theories. As a result, we find that magnetic fields with a torsional wave speed lower than the local sound speed do not induce spiral arms in the disk.

Data mining and knowledge management have led to the development of association rule-based methods, which have received significant attention, particularly in the fields of data mining, logic, and linguistics. A wide range of logics and linguistic frameworks have been introduced to model association rules, each with its unique characteristics. This paper offers a unifying framework that integrates multiple theories on association rules. The framework builds upon repetition orders, a recently developed mathematical structure, to provide a comprehensive foundation. By integrating the concepts of logic and linguistics, the framework allows for comparing and combining existing theories, which in turn enables proving minimum-size bases for association rules. As a result, the framework contributes to establishing first-order logic as equivalent to arm-strong logic, and it yields a new, concise basis for multivariate linguistic association rules.

The number of people going through the criminal justice system has been steadily rising, creating a substantial group that often suffers from severe mental illness.  Although first offenders tend to show minor symptoms of mental disorders, recidivists frequently display clear signs of psychological disorders, necessitating rehabilitation and psychological treatment to prevent future crimes and improve their social functioning.  A crucial step in addressing the mental health needs of offenders is the legal system mandating psychological treatment, a measure that is increasingly adopted by courts worldwide, including in Brazil.  In the context of Brazilian law, the psychological evaluation of offenders is a legal requirement, and the system's implementation has been in place for over two decades, with the goal of using these evaluations to make treatment a court-ordered condition for offenders.  Despite the long-standing implementation of this treatment in the Brazilian system, there is a lack of evidence-based research on the effectiveness of these treatments in changing offenders' behaviors.  To address this knowledge gap, a study was conducted to assess the impact of court-ordered psychological treatments on recidivism rates, with the objective of evaluating whether these treatments can reduce recidivism and reinforcing their importance in psychological and legal communities.  A difference-in-differences analysis was conducted using a large dataset of over 130,000 offenders in Brazil, separated into two categories: those ordered to undergo treatment and those who were not ordered to undergo treatment.  The results showed that recidivism among those who underwent court-ordered psychological

A new class of Apostol–Bernoulli polynomials of the second kind with parameters is defined, along with its associated polynomials and key characteristics, including functional equations, an expansion theorem, and relationships with special types of Bernoulli and Apostol–Ferrandini polynomials. Various identities related to this new class are also derived.

Radio mapping has become a popular approach for network planning and optimization by directing drones to collect data on signal strength from various locations. This data is then used to generate a 3D map of the environment's coverage. This paper delves into assuring the quality of this radio map by defining and analyzing its structural characteristics and variability. By applying statistical theory, we define and measure the smoothness and randomness of the map, and develop an algorithm to assess the drone flight path required to create an accurate, quality-assured radio map. This research shifts the focus from a single data point accuracy, as traditionally emphasized, to ensuring the overall quality of the radio map.

To effectively monitor industrial equipment, our research proposes a novelty-driven identification method for anomaly detection and classification. This means our approach focuses on identifying anomalies based on how much they deviate from normal operating patterns, rather than relying on pre-existing examples of anomalies. Our proposed method combines traditional probability evaluation with modern feature extraction techniques to develop simple and interpretable statistical models for multivariate time series data. Specifically, our study validates the merits of using hidden Markov models in conjunction with the use of complex models such as autoencoders for dimensionality reduction and feature creation that better reflect the underlying structure of time-series data. As a result, our analysis shows that our proposed HMM-GPE approach, combined with a novel complexity metric, outperforms alternative anomaly detection methods on public data sets and by leveraging the HMM's probabilistic structure, our approach provides meaningful likelihood scores that accurately gauge the severity of anomalies, making it practical for real-world applications.

This research proposes a comprehensive system for identifying individuals through their voice, facial features, and thermal images. Each modality utilizes specific deep learning architectures, followed by the combination of their respective features using an attention-based approach to enhance overall recognition capabilities. The proposed system was evaluated using the CACD, VCTK, and RIKEN-IPD datasets, yielding an exceptional average accuracy of 99.21% across all datasets. Furthermore, this study investigates the impact of varying sensing distances on authentication performance and offers a theoretical explanation for these findings.

When it comes to statistical learning, having more data is generally beneficial, but collecting large amounts of data can be costly. Fortunately, there are several low-cost ways to artificially increase your data supply by processing what you already have. These methods include creating reverse video for augmentation, back-translation, and reverse translation for language models. However, our research shows that these techniques have largely been ignored in automatic speech recognition and translation. We introduce three novel methods that rely on very little extra computation to increase your data, and find that using them can be comparable to having 2-5 times more audio for language models created with modern architectures.

Consider a set of observations denoted as $y_1,\ldots, y_n$, where each observation corresponds to a discrete distribution defined as $\sum_{j=1}^{k} p_{0,j}(y)y_{0,j}(y)$, with $p_{0,j}(y)$ representing the probability density function of the $j$-th component and $p_{0,j}$ representing the average of the $j$-th component. Our objective is to estimate the quantity $\sum_{j=1}^{k} p_{0,j}(y)$ for any given $y$. In the context of finite mixtures where $k$ is finite and the set of possible values for $y$ is countable, a maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) exists and can be expressed as the average of the parameter space $\mathcal{P}$ for any given $y$, provided that the set of possible values for $y$ is countable. Furthermore, a similar result can be proven for infinite mixtures. In sampling applications, the estimated parameter is used to calculate the finite population size, and the variance of the estimator can be expressed in terms of the Fisher information. In the context of continuous and semicontinuous distributions, the variance of the estimator can be expressed in terms of the Fisher information. In the discrete case, the estimator can be computed in a finite number of steps, whereas in the continuous case, the estimator can be computed in a finite

Building on the one-sided differential privacy (ODP) model, which offers a formal guarantee for protecting an individual's confidential information, research has focused on quantifying the risk of leakage for collective characteristics. However, a crucial aspect often overlooked in this model is the protection of non-aggregate features, such as the specific order of data within a characteristic. This paper examines the risk of leakage from characteristic samples under ODP, using a framework that measures privacy loss based on mutual information between an attacker and characteristic samples, given a fixed dataset. Our findings reveal that even without revealing aggregate information, an ODP model can inadvertently expose confidential details through the characteristic's underlying structure, and we provide numerical examples to substantiate this observation. To address this issue, we propose a novel model called one-sided group-sampled differential privacy (GSDP), which offers improved confidentiality for both individual and sampled characteristics. Our research also validates the feasibility of GSDP through simulations on two datasets, demonstrating its practical applicability.

We have obtained high-resolution ALMA images of the AS 209 protoplanetary disk to study its inner structure. A gap was discovered in $^{12}$CO emission at a distance of approximately 12-60 AU from the central star. This finding confirms the presence of a gap detected in millimeter continuum emission. The outer boundary of the gap aligns with a warped ring, and both features may be caused by a single migrating planet. Analysis of gas-to-dust ratio suggests that the density of gas within the gap could still be significant, and future observations using shorter wavelengths or molecular lines with higher excitation energies are necessary to better constrain its density. Alternatively, the gap could not be purely physical, and the apparent lack of gas could be due to processing of molecules as they migrate inward from the outer ring.

An analysis of time-sensitive data is an essential aspect of numerous cutting-edge scientific and industrial techniques, such as fluorescence correlation spectroscopy, analysis of single molecules, ion tracking, and counting photons, among others. In this study, we introduce a versatile software solution, referred to as 'trackmenuplugin', which aids in furthering these applications by providing analysis functions focused on tracking, visibility analysis, and correlation calculations. This tool integrates seamlessly with the medmenupackage for simulation and data simulation management, which can be accessed via the Virtual Organon Platform by Virtual Techniques GmbH.

For a class of mean field games with controls, where the state space is constrained to a closed convex subset of R^d, we demonstrate that, given standard regularity and growth conditions on the Hame尔顿ian and velocity function, a mild solution exists and is unique in the space of continuous functions.

We investigate the underlying framework of the disk's evolution by applying a novel approach that separates disk stars into various populations based on their age, metallicity, and distance, utilizing Gaia data from the first data release. These different populations are then used to identify patterns in the disk's development over time and 3D structure changes. Our analysis shows that previously identified "threads" in phase space are not uniform across all stellar populations, are likely formed due to numerical issues rather than being the primary evolution mechanism, and are only prevalent in young, less metallic stars. Instead, we propose a model where the different star populations in the disk are connected through age and metallicity rather than being part of a unified structure. Our findings also indicate that the gap between inner and outer disk populations in action space is more pronounced and cannot be accounted for by a single quasi-continuous structure. Our evolution model successfully reproduishes the distribution of different stellar populations in action space, and our analysis of the high-metallicity old disk populations reveals that their present structure is a combination of their past locations and present ages. Our work lays the groundwork for incorporating these diverse stellar populations into machine learning algorithms to enhance our understanding of the disk's evolution.

Recent advancements in deep learning have enabled the rise of Visual Discrepancy Detection (VDD), which seeks to distinguish reliable inferences from unreliable ones. Most current methods for VDD are effective for numerical or image classification tasks but face significant challenges when applied to more complex tasks such as detecting visual inconsistencies. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a new approach called VICTOR. It leverages transformers and contrastive pre-training, which are adapted for real-world applications and the specific needs of the fashion industry. We demonstrate the effectiveness of VICTOR in detecting visual inconsistencies within fashion images, achieving superior results compared to existing methods. Additionally, it provides insightful feature-level visualization that helps users understand the characteristics of reliable visual observations. The proposed technique, training data, and code can be accessed at https://github.com/Cheng-CH/VICTOR.

Recent advancements in experimental technology have enabled the development of sophisticated
  light sources that can produce complex states of generalized classical and quantum nature. This has spurred
  interest in exploring new forms of light-based computation that harness the properties of these non-classical
  light sources. Research in this area is known as photonic resource theory. This survey will provide an
  accessible overview, targeting a broad audience including experimentalists and theorists, by presenting
  fundamental concepts in the mathematical description of non-classical light. It will also introduce the
  foundational principles of resource theory as applied to various computation models and specific applications
  in information processing. Furthermore, it will review existing literature on photonic resource theory to
  illustrate its potential in developing novel schemes for information processing.

A key challenge in federated learning is that its central server must manage a vast number of client connections. To address this, servers typically employ an asynchronous accumulation strategy, allowing multiple clients to submit updates simultaneously. However, this approach can lead to bias in the model convergence. This paper examines how asynchronous accumulation affects the model convergence in federated learning, and finds that, in buffered accumulation, the delay introduced can actually improve convergence. Following this discovery, a new method called BuFL is proposed to boost the efficiency of asynchronous federated learning. BuFL optimizes the server's resource usage and minimizes the model bias, and experimental results demonstrate its superiority over existing approaches.

This study investigates a theory of operational calculus that combines partial differential operators with constant coefficients and differential equations that involve the Laplacian operator. It further explores the properties of generalized functions, specifically those that are polynomially bounded, and examines their behavior under differentiation and convolution with polynomial and exponential functions. Building upon a previously established theory, this study adapts it to work within a broader mathematical framework, allowing for a more comprehensive analysis of differential equations and their solutions.

A hypothesis from recent AdS/CFT research suggests that the dimension of the universe might be perceived as having an additional, hidden aspect, potentially resolving issues with quantum gravity. We investigate whether this hidden dimension could be the source of the dark matter, particularly the portion that constitutes the majority of the universe's matter. According to our calculations, the condition for primordial black holes to constitute the entire matter portion of the universe is strictly limited to a narrow range, thereby disqualifying a particular class of dark hole models.

Scientific experiments demonstrate that soap and lemon oil films exhibit elastic behavior when stretched, forming a crystalline structure, known as tilt crystals, in the case of soap films. When the film's stretching exceeds its elastic limit, it ruptures, often in a way that resembles the fracture patterns seen in metals. This rupture can be initiated at a point where the film's structural crystals become disordered, known as a defect, and is influenced by factors such as surface texture, frame movement, and impurities. The fracture pattern can be predicted using an equation, but the process of rupture is not uniform, as it can begin in one location and later in another, and is influenced by the way the film is moved during stretching.

The main issue hindering the widespread use of gallium nitride (GaN) is its low electrical mobility, particularly its anisotropic and strain-sensitive properties in nitride heterostructures. To address this, researchers investigated the strain effects on GaN's properties when aligned with the crystal lattice of ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$. These two materials have similar lattice sizes to GaN, allowing for the application of uniaxial strain without introducing additional stress. By utilizing ab-initio calculations, the study found that GaN's anisotropic strain could enhance its anisotropy factor as much as 10 times, resulting in a 4.4 times increase in hole mobility compared to conventional GaN. These discoveries suggest a new method for improving GaN's performance and potentially utilizing GaN in new applications.

Our research focuses on addressing the navigation issue in the complex and changing environment of the marine ecosystem. The dynamic nature of the marine environment makes robot navigation extremely challenging, thus necessitating the development of advanced techniques. To this end, we propose a novel Gaussian Process model that leverages the sparsity principle to capture the pattern of the underlying function, as well as its rate of change, through the structure of the covariance matrix. The proposed model is then utilized in model-based control to facilitate navigation of the robot, as well as to learn the fundamental properties of the underlying function, as well as its rate of change. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated by comparing it to traditional Gaussian Process models and by showing that our approach facilitates more efficient and accurate navigation of the robot.

We establish new formulas enabling the computation of the Merazka invariant for isothermal surfaces, which in turn allows for the extension of the 19-century findings of Darboux and Calapso transformations.

Nonparametric regression offers an alternative to traditional parametric estimation,
eliminating the need for restrictive assumptions about functional forms.
However, when dealing with multiple covariates, series expansions like polynomials
or sines and cosines, series expansions can provide precisely the same fit as the
data while being computationally efficient. On the other hand, kernel methods offer
an alternative, but they struggle with the "curse of dimensionality," making
estimation in the presence of many covariates infeasible. Moreover, kernel
smoothing can inadvertently introduce spurious periodicity into the data.
To address these issues, a new series estimation method is introduced, leveraging
the properties of Chebyshev polynomials to offer a series expansion that converges
uniformly and efficiently, even with a relatively small number of terms.
This uniform convergence property enables the use of series estimation even with
a relatively modest number of terms, resulting in improved efficiency
and exploitation of the smoothing effect without the drawbacks of periodicity.
The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through simulations and a real-world
analysis of U.S. state crime rates, confirming its versatility and reliability.

This paper examines the $\lambda$-versions of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind and explores their relationships and identities. We discuss how these versions relate to other $\lambda$-Stirling numbers, as well as their connections to the $\lambda$-Bell numbers and numbers associated with partitions into groups of at least $r+1$. The paper also includes connections to $\lambda$-permutation cycles and a new set of identities involving these numbers.

Predicting evolving relationships within a growing set of data is crucial in many fields, yet this task is complicated by incomplete existing relationships and irregular temporal patterns. Although previous studies have used static frameworks for predicting temporal relationships, they have not thoroughly examined their effectiveness or compared them to more advanced models. In this study, we investigate the performance of static frameworks for predicting temporal relationships and how it is impacted by data sparsity and granularity. Additionally, we contrast their performance with that of advanced models using neural networks, taking into account the characteristics of the training data. Our investigation involved creating two new datasets as well as utilizing an existing one, allowing us to draw several significant conclusions.

A fundamental concept in the theory of dynamical systems and operator algebras is the notion of shift equivalence, especially after Cuntz expanded it to operator algebras and graph algebras in the 1970s. This concept underwent further development over the following decades, ultimately leading to an extension for a broader class of graphs in 2015 by Kim and Zhang. This extension robust shift equivalence, for finite graphs, was operator-algebraically significant as it represented distinct classes. This paper aims to provide a purely graph-theoretic definition of robust shift equivalence, applicable to infinite graphs. Additionally, we establish that the robust shift equivalence classes of finite graphs with operator-algebraic Cuntz-Krieger sets in mind can be determined. Our work also shows that the operator algebras associated with a finite graph's shift equivalence are robust shift equivalent, thereby extending the concept to graph algebras.

In the quark-gluon plasma under influence of a magnetic field, the direction of the field alters the direction of particle movement, thus modifying propagators and affecting observables. This research examines how the magnetic fieldwikki affects the creation of quark-antiquark pairs, or jet production, in heavy quark fragmentation. We incorporate the impact of electromagnetic fields on propagators and vertex functions in calculating quark-antiquark pair production rates and explore the resulting anisotropy in jet production as a function of angle with respect to the quark's direction. Our investigation also extends to jet production of electrically neutral particles, such as photons and neutral mesons, in the presence of a magnetic field.

Recent advances in language modeling have enabled models to answer complex questions, but they struggle with queries that require logical reasoning over a knowledge base. Although some methods tackle this issue, they often neglect leveraging structured knowledge graphs, which contain pre-defined logical relationships between entities. This study demonstrates that integrating symbolic reasoning into language models significantly improves its question-answering capabilities, especially when answering queries that involve logical inference. Specifically, we found that using the TransE model for reasoning and incorporating its integrated knowledge into the language modeling process yields positive results on the WebQSP dataset, a challenging question-answer dataset derived from Wikipedia.

In this paper, we explore the properties of high-dimensional expanders and their relevant structures, specifically using covers to determine novel examples. Our investigation reveals that certain types of structures, such as products, bipartite expansions, and random constructions, serve as robust sources of high-dimensional expanders. Additionally, we demonstrate that both the Kneser graph and its variant yield notable high-dimensional expanders. Our analysis also incorporates technical contributions concerning the calculations and expansions of homology in the resulting complexes.

This study investigates the effectiveness of carefully designed input data, known as
prompts, on the performance of large language models, specifically focusing on their
ability to generate accurate answers without prior training. We examine the broad
influence of prompt design on model outcomes, revealing significant variations in
results. We also pinpoint specific aspects of the prompt that can substantially
improve the quality of the model's responses. Our analysis across diverse datasets
demonstrates the critical role of human-like language in the prompt in unlocking the
full potential of these language models.

For a class of artin motives with Kummer-dedekind base change, we identify and study a family of l-invariants. We establish that these invariants form a structured, one-dimensional module, governed by an elusive, yet intrinsic, l-adic character. Furthermore, by examining specific cases, such as Hida families of p-ordinary p-eigenclasses of p-scalar-weight two newforms and certain/pseudo/Pisert newforms, we evaluate if the rank of this module's Hida family rank determines its rank, thereby drawing connections to long-standing major conjectures in the field, including the main conjecture of Iwasawa for arbitrary odd nonCM forms and the Rankin-Selberg Conjecture for unitary group.

In experiments with Rydberg atoms, microwave fields can be detected with high precision using optical or mm-wave light, or even less-well-resolved frequencies like visible light, thanks to the extensive electronic transitions in Rydberg atoms. Experiments typically use Rydberg atom ensembles for signal amplification, yielding significant improvements in sensitivity, accessible from the single-photon limit with sensors as small as a cubic micrometer. However, the Rydberg state is vulnerable to depletion due to light scattering, limiting the coherence time. To rectify this, a machine learning algorithm, specifically deep learning, is now being used to enhance the detection of multifrequency microwave signals. This improvement stems from applying a digital filter trained in simulation to the Rydberg-based detector, optimizing the detection method and mitigating the impact of detector limitations. This novel technique is expected to enhance microwave detection using Rydberg atom clouds.

UGC8839, a nearby spiral galaxy, possesses an unusually thick and uniformly bright central region. This study presents a novel, comprehensive analysis of UGC8839's properties. By examining its properties across a range of wavelengths from ultraviolet to near-infrared, researchers identified that UC8839 has a stellar metallicity of approximately 0.24 times that of the Sun. UC8839 exhibits a relatively slow rotation of about 100 km/s and a high radial gradient of its metallicity. This is the first time that a comprehensive analysis of UC8839's properties has been presented. UC8839 is characterized by its high metallicity, moderate rotation, and radial gradient in its central compact starburst region. UC8839's unusual structure may be attributed to a recent, massive inflow of gas that triggered a rapid starburst. This study provides a framework for understanding the relationship between the spiral galaxy's properties and its underlying physical processes.

This study demonstrates that the $H^{top}(\mathcal{J})$ dimension of a non-linear elliptic quasiregular mapping's hyperbolic set $\mathcal{J}$ cannot exceed its topological dimension. For a related class of super-elliptic mappings, we establish the exact topological dimension of $\mathcal{J}$ as described by H. Ojala in 2008. Furthermore, we investigate conditions under which $\mathcal{J}$'s topological dimension equals $n-1$.

Mars' atmospheric gravity waves play a significant role in driving and heating the upper atmosphere, making their characteristics crucial to understanding the planet's gravity wave dynamics. To achieve this, researchers utilize various approaches to analyze the temporal and spatial behavior of gravity waves, including their amplitude variations, wavelength changes, phase velocity, and propagation direction. In our study, we investigate how past MGS, ODY, MRO, and MAVEN observations have contributed to our understanding of Mars' gravity waves, particularly in how they affect the planet's crustal induction and ionization. Moreover, we examine how these waves affect different altitudes in the thermosphere, as well as their spatial and temporal behavior, and how their properties vary in different regions of the planet. Our research provides valuable insights into the gravity wave dynamics on Mars, which is critical for various applications, including modeling the planet's crustal induction and ionization.

The LHC has demonstrated its capability for generating massive quantities of photons, an phenomenon attributed to the intense electromagnetic fields produced by nuclei. Researchers have utilized these photons as a powerful tool to investigate nuclear interactions in a unique state, referred to as an ultra-peripheral nucleus-nucleus collision. Recent studies by the ALICE collaboration at CERN's 2018 run have focused on examining forward J/psi production, both within and outside the forward detector range, in both lead-lead and proton-lead collisions. Analyzing this data provides valuable insights into the essential parameters of photon-nucleon cross-sections and nuclear structure function $F_2$ at extremely low values of $x$ and high photon virtualities.

In response to the limitations of current sound design approaches, we introduce an innovative system that enables sound designers to produce complex, audio textures by visually guiding a neural network. This advanced tool combines the power of neural network-based sound synthesis with the simplicity of image editing, allowing designers to modify existing audio by altering image components. By leveraging convolutional neural networks and differential audio synthesis, our system achieves high-quality, coherent sound output. We showcase the system's effectiveness and user-friendly interface, resulting in a wide range of novel audio textures.

In numerous applications, particularly with clinical data, it's often beneficial
to consider time as a crucial factor. This research introduces a novel approach,
called Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NEODIE), leveraging recurrent
neural networks to produce continuous outputs along a timeline. By employing
an attention mechanism, we can generate varying levels of focus on distinct
time points when making predictions. Our proposed method is specifically
tailored for predicting progression-free survival in glioblastoma patients from
the Clinical Trials database. We compare our method with alternative approaches
and demonstrate that it achieves superior results, achieving an AUC of 0.752.
Additionally, we analyze patients across different time points to extract
readable conclusions. Our research reveals initial treatment's significance in
the early stages, while genetic mutations like EGFR and PTEN loss become
more influential later on. Our findings are corroborated by medical experts.
Notably, we discover that different genetic mutations have disparate impacts
at various time points. This method offers an innovative way to work with
grainy data obtained from multiple clinical visits. Our approach outperforms
existing methods in predicting progression-free survival and provides valuable
insights into various time periods.

A fundamental concept underlies all our pandemic intervention strategies - the need to intervene promptly to mitigate human suffering.  However, a critical aspect often overlooked in our policy discussions is the specific moment at which our interventions should begin to have optimal effects.  Our research fills this knowledge gap by introducing the precise solution concept, introducing mathematical modeling to identify precise intervention moments that minimize economic loss and human mortality simultaneously.  By applying this model to eight different scenarios, we demonstrate its broad applicability and provide clear guidance on when to implement precise measures, effectively resolving a major conflict between human life and economic interests in the process.  Our analysis indicates that the precise solution often falls within the range of current policy guidelines, underscoring the importance of timely action to achieve beneficial outcomes for all parties involved.  Our precise solution concept can serve as a unifying framework for decision-making across a range of contexts, effectively addressing complex trade-offs and guiding policy in the pandemic and beyond.

A critical phase in machine learning model development involves verifying model performance, particularly when issues arise, such as subpar accuracy or unexpected behavior. However, pinpointing the underlying cause of these problems can be a complex task. In this research, we introduce Shapley Importance, a novel approach rooted in Shapley values, to identify the most influential data elements and model components within a machine learning pipeline. By applying Shapley Importance, we can effectively highlight the most significant factors contributing to model performance variations. Our method has been successfully applied to optimize image classification models on the CIFAR-10 dataset by using it to detect anomalies in the data, and by retraining the model with the filtered anomalies, we achieved improved results. Furthermore, Shapley Importance can be used across various model types and affectable pipeline stages, making it a versatile tool for machine learning pipeline optimization.

This paper begins by presenting an introduction to the core concepts of cocharge, derived from a lecture given at Queen Mary University of London in 2018. It then details how to count minors within matrices, revealing an insightful interpretation through the lens of cocharge. Furthermore, the paper explores the application of multivariate polynomials in solving problems related to geometry within matrices. Additionally, we outline a novel approach to understanding topological patterns within matrices, connecting them to a concept called the cohomology ring.

Our study reveals the application of high pressure as a tool for adjusting both magnetic and electronic properties in Mn$_3$Sn, an anomalous helimagnet. Experiments conducted using a resistivity measurement technique in a high-pressure device showed that a pressure of around 3.5 GPa eliminates the anomalous Hall effect and drives a magnetic phase transition in Mn$_3$Sn, transforming its triangular antiferromagnetism into ferrimagnetism. At low temperatures, the resistance of Mn$_3$Sn under high pressure conditions exhibits a semi-conducting behavior, while the magnetic phase transition is accompanied by changes in scattering mechanisms. A theoretical model suggests that the driving force behind Mn$_3$Sn's triangular antiferromagnetism-to-ferrimagnetism transition can be attributed to lattice distortions affecting its inter-layer distances.

A novel framework for detailed relationship extraction in clinical texts, particularly concerning seizures, has been developed. This approach utilizes a network of neural connections for classification, paired with an effective method for producing human-readable explanations. The framework automatically generates insights into the training process and desired relationships, thereby facilitating the identification of relevant patterns for extraction. Additionally, a second layer of analysis refines the model's output by assessing the connections between input variables, thereby enhancing the accuracy of the extracted relationships. The approach was tested on two datasets of varying quality. This high-quality dataset was meticulously annotated by experienced epileptologists, whereas the lower-quality dataset lacked clear boundaries for the entities and their connections. Notably, the approach demonstrated exceptional performance on the expert-annotated dataset, correctly identifying 94% of the relationships. Furthermore, the system was able to achieve 70% accuracy in scenarios with less precise annotations, significantly outperforming traditional techniques.

This paper examines a joint eigenvalue problem that combines Steklov and Robin boundary conditions. Specifically, we focus on the boundary conditions $\frac{\partial u}{\partial n} + \beta u = 0$ and $v = \gamma v$, where $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are real parameters. We investigate the properties of the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem, and demonstrate the existence of infinite sequences of normalized pairs of eigenvalues $(\lambda_n^{(\beta,\gamma)}, \mu_n^{(\beta,\gamma)})$ and corresponding normalized eigenfunctions $(\phi_{n,j}^{(\beta,\gamma)})$. The study reveals that the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions depend continuously on the boundary parameters $\beta$ and $\gamma$. Furthermore, we derive explicit formulas for the eigenvalues in the cases of particularly simple domains, such as rectangles and triangles.

Reconstructing hypergraphs from their sampled data is a valuable approach in multiple fields, such as biology and social science. This paper presents an efficient algorithm that uses a small number of samples to accurately rebuild the original hypergraph. This algorithm leverages a new concept called hypergraph conductance and relies on simple, scalable techniques from graph theory. Moreover, the algorithm can be applied to hypergraphs defined by complex, high-dimensional data and even when the sample distribution differs from the original population. Extensive tests on both simulated and real-world data have shown that the proposed method outperforms existing techniques.

This study proposes an innovative approach to understanding computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) by using radiologists' annotations to identify the location and nature of diseases in chest X-rays.  A novel algorithm is employed to leverage computed tomography scans to create these X-ray projections, which are then used in conjunction with radiologists' feedback to create detailed correspondences between CT and X-ray images.  These annotations provide invaluable insights for the analysis and detection of diseases in chest X-rays, which are essential for the development of effective CAD systems.

The Thurston norm is calculated for Euler characteristic zero characteristic submanifolds of contact structures that are tight and defined on certain types of three-dimensional spaces. The underlying manifolds can be described as connected sums of specific geometric structures, including those found in certain types of three-dimensional surfaces and linked knots.

The behavior of directional emitters in 2D laser arrays is analyzed using a statistical approach for their spatial distribution within a box-shaped area. An entropy-based model reveals the presence of gauge symmetries in the probability model, influencing the directional emission model through methods like variational principles. These techniques enable the creation of self-consistent models without relying on traditional minimization methods. Additionally, a method for calculating the probability of combined states in the array is developed, incorporating effects from both directional emission patterns and the number of active lasers in the system. This approach yields closed-form expressions for the probability density function and entropy, revealing an inverse relationship between these properties. These model properties are subsequently compared with experimental data from Unger et al. in 2019.

A primary requirement for a cryptocurrency to be considered a reliable store of value and transactional medium is its price stability. This study investigates the price stability of all cryptocurrencies in circulation as of this writing, utilizing a comprehensive approach that combines econometric techniques and ranking methods to evaluate whether individual cryptocurrencies' prices remain stable over various periods and currencies, including the US dollar, euro, and Chinese yuan. By applying established methodology first introduced for traditional currencies by Izhakian and Levy, this research identifies four cryptocurrencies with persistent prices: Bitshares, Peercoin, Decred, and Navcoin. The results indicate that the majority of cryptocurrencies exhibit significant volatility and cannot be used as a store of value. However, certain cryptocurrencies show lower volatility when evaluated in non-Western currencies, suggesting that the influence of Western political and economic factors on their prices may be less pronounced.

We develop a feeble noise theory of the KP equation by combining the direct method with an inverse method, specifically reverse scattering. This approach feeble noise theory can effectively deal with arbitrary nonlinearity coefficients and is valid in a small noise limit. By solving the inverse scattering problem in the reverse direction, we obtain a complete set of soliton and radiation data that fully describe the evolution of the KP soliton equation. Specifically, we present a detailed analytical solution to the Cauchy problem for the Fokas solution class, resulting in a complex nonlinear superposition principle for scattering parameters. This principle allows us to describe the evolution of soliton phases, phases asymptotically, and radiation, which provides a comprehensive description of the KP soliton equation's evolution, outperforming other feeble noise theories.

The MMS mission's observations of the solar wind have provided valuable insights into compressive turbulent fluctuations at sub-ion scales. Analysis of multi-spacecraft data collected during a single solar wind interval has demonstrated that these fluctuations exhibit similar characteristics to both Kolmogorov's 5/3 power law and the recently proposed 3/2 power law at various scales. However, the scales where the 3/2 power law becomes applicable are significantly larger than the ion-cyclotron radius and close to the electron-cyclotron radius. This suggests that the fluctuating magnetic field spectra observed by MMS are influenced by kinetic-scale effects dominated by ions and electrons. Moreover, the MMS data show that the ion-cyclotron and electron-cyclotron radii coincide with the scales that mark the transition between the inertial and kinetic regimes, and this transition is influenced by the ion and electron temperatures and the angle between the magnetic field and the line-of-sight.

Slicing ultra-short pulses into sub-cycle bursts can be achieved by applying a specific modulation to the SASE process, resulting in an attosecond train linked to each peak intensity. Utilizing a changed approach, a single burst can be isolated to produce attosecond-duration pulses. This work involves applying a focused electron sheet with a modified radial momentum profile to filter the FEL or HGHRL output, creating attosecond pulses at various wavelengths from XUV to soft X-ray.

Physically based models predict that shear forces in certain types of fluid flows will increase instability and turbulence as the fluid's viscosity decreases below a critical threshold. This type of fluid dynamics is modeled using the forrester-levermore physical estimation method, which is an efficient way to compute one-dimensional shear forces in layered fluids. By assuming that the fluid's velocity and pressure can be represented as exponential functions, the model provides a faster alternative to more computationally intensive numerical simulations, which is particularly useful for climate and geophysical simulations. The new research expands this model to include the effects of fluid viscosity and demonstrates that the model maintains high accuracy with low computational costs.

Our research introduces two evaluation metrics for detecting unfair political districting plans. The first metric, \textit{partisan heating}, quantifies the extent of strategic manipulation by a party during districting. A second metric, \textit{heating}, is designed to be neutral to any particular party and can identify unusual districting patterns even when no party is being unfairly targeted. These metrics are paired with a similarity-based districting method, ensuring that the resulting districts balance closeness to an unbiased reference plan with a minimum level of the introduced heating. We extensively tested our methods using simulated voting data and real voting data, and found our approach to uncover highly unfair districting plans created during two US redistricting events. We also used our methods to propose alternative, more fair districting plans. The code for our methods is publicly accessible on our GitHub repository: \url{https://github.com/robertsreeks/gerry}.

The increasing importance of patterned textiles in fashion and production quality control necessitates advanced flaw detection methods. To address this, a new scheme is proposed that combines the Geometric Hashing Graphox and low-rank decomposition techniques. By leveraging the self-repeating patterned nature of textile images, the approach develops a block comparison graph that captures the relationships between image segments. Subsequently, the associated matrix is analyzed using low-rank decomposition to amplify minor defects and segment the image into distinct regions. Each region is then evaluated using the GHGO algorithm, which rectifies any inconsistencies, and anomalies are pinpointed based on the deviation of certain features from the median. By testing the approach on various flaw types, including tears, stains, and pattern irregularities, the results demonstrate its effectiveness, and the analysis highlights its potential applications in textile quality inspections.

Recent advances in regulation learning have demonstrated its effectiveness in enhancing sample efficiency and exploration quality in remote control learning. However, integrating RL with precise motion control remains challenging, particularly in the context of autonomous navigation. Unlike traditional navigation methods that rely on image features, the policy in image-based navigation produces orientation commands, leaving the actual movement to a navigator, whose control laws are difficult to adjust due to the discontinuous nature of the orientation signal. We propose a new approach that decouples the navigation agent and the navigator, allowing for independent development and optimized performance, particularly in aerial vehicle deployment. We further introduce a novel cost function that encourages the regulation policy to retain as much uncertainty as possible, thus promoting beneficial exploration for both agents. Through thorough simulations and real-world aerial vehicle tests, we show that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods, yielding more efficient training, higher success rates, and increased robustness.

This study examines whether a certain type of gravitational mass increase poses a conflict with another type of mass decrease known as the Bondi mass reduction. By analyzing the initial constraints imposed by Einstein's equations on time-dependent changes in the metric, we derive an upper limit for the rate at which Bondi mass can decrease in terms of the cube of certain spatial characteristics and a measure of time variation in the gravitational field. Specifically, the bondi mass reduction rate is limited to being less than or equal to $E^3$, where $E$ represents a combination of the characteristics. This result follows directly from the initial constraints and does not rely on broader assumptions about spacetime regularity.

The initial population of stars, formed in massive early galaxies, likely collapsed into dense clusters at their galactic centers. In the ensuing environment, the subsequent star populations inherited these compact configurations, giving rise to numerous loose binaries and clusters of stars in the process. In the absence of supernovae explosions to disperse them, these objects have continued to emit gravitational waves for billions of years. In the future, the interplay between these objects through gravitational interactions will lead to the formation of the first hard binaries, capable of generating detectable signals with LIGO. By simulating these scenarios, we find a wide range of possibilities for the generation of gravitational waves, heavily influenced by assumptions about the initial conditions. However, some of these predictions may align with the observed properties of galaxies, implying that some of the signals generated could originate within galaxies we observe today.

In modern power distribution grids equipped with energy storage systems and flexible loads, traditional methods of identifying short-circuit incidents using overcurrent protection are becoming unreliable. This is largely due to the nuanced patterns of curtailment that can mimic the effects of actual incidents, complicating the distinction between the two. This challenge is further compounded by the need for precise data to effectively differentiate between the curtailment of incidents, which demands a deeper understanding of system dynamics and state variables. This paper presents an innovative data-driven method for reliably identifying short-circuit incidents in distribution grids, even in the absence of detailed system models. By focusing on the effects of incident-induced fluctuations in system variables, our approach is designed to provide a clear distinction between real incidents and controlled curtailment activities. This is achieved through the analysis of temporal relationships between fluctuation magnitude and system dynamics, as well as the speed at which fluctuations occur following the event's onset. This understanding of geometric and topological dynamics plays a pivotal role in the success of our method. Extensive simulations based on detailed EMTP models have validated the efficacy of our method in various scenarios.

Our study focuses on the decay process of the X(3872) resonance, and we utilize
the framework of chiral perturbation theory to investigate its interactions with
lighter resonances such as $J/\psi$, $\pi$, and $\pi\pi$. A crucial assumption is
the inclusion of a derivative coupling between the X(3872) and these lighter
resonances. By applying unitarization to the X(3872)-$D^0 \bar D^{*0}$ system,
we determine the transition amplitude for the process $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi
\pi \gamma$. Additionally, considering the X(3872) as a bound state of a charm
quark and a charm antiquark, we consider the processes $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi
\pi$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi$ as quark annihilation processes.
Calculations of transition amplitudes for these processes are consistent with both
experimental data on the $X(3872\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma)$ decay and recent
measurements of the $X(3872\rightarrow J/\psi \pi$ and $X(3872\rightarrow J/\psi
\pi\pi)$ decays. A comparison of our results with alternative theoretical

We define specific categories $\mathbb{Q}^{(d)}$ that encapsulate information about smooth quadrics for dimensions $d \geq 0$, and demonstrate their relation to categories associated with singular quadrics. This allows us to reconstruct the defining equations of smooth quadrics from their associated categories, thereby encompassing a category theory version of the classical result that distinct non-isotropic quadratic forms are equivalent. For $d = 0$, the category $\mathbb{Q}^{(0)}$ is set to be the zero category, whereas $\mathbb{Q}^{(1)}$ comprises the tilting module category of a tame tilting algebra. Additionally, we show that $\mathbb{Q}^{(2)}$ can be described as a quotient category derived from a hereditary order.

TextWorldExpress is a groundbreaking multi-language, make-my-text environment that enables the simulation of basic text-based games. Its innovative design incorporates a made-up language with unique properties such as an established vocabulary, logical structure, state tracking system, and pre-defined game objectives with predictable solutions. In a real-world application, TextWorldExpress has successfully applied machine learning techniques like supervised and imitation training to solve complex problems within games like Cooking Adventure. By utilizing these techniques, TextWorldExpress has achieved impressive results, including a generation time of one million steps per second and access to human demonstrations at the same speed.

To circumvent potential issues related to topological defects, we propose a novel method for defining geometric phases in topological insulators, independent of spatial coordinates. This approach enables us to precisely calculate the electric field and magnetic flux generated by a slowly moving charge. In particular, our method confirms the mathematical relationship between these phases, showing they equal the integrated electric and magnetic fields, thus validating Stokes' theorem at the level of geometric phases. Additionally, our findings indicate that the magnetic flux value depends on the topological magneto-electric response. The proposed method has been mathematically verified for topological insulators containing topological defects, and our results can be generalized to systems with arbitrary structures.

For the p-Laplace equation, we derive several estimates in sectors of the plane and demonstrate how they translate into boundary gradient estimates for p-positive non-degenerate functions. These estimates also enable us to prove a mean value formula in sectors, which further allows us to establish a precise formula for asymptotically p-log-concave functions in planar domains. Our approach is based on the introduction of a sector-specific measure of convexity and the construction of a vector field with specific properties. These innovations provide novel insights even in the case of uniformly convex sectors.

This research introduces a novel spatial extreme value model that uses multivariate Generalized Pareve distributions to describe peak values at multiple locations, given a peak value at a specific site. The study applies the model to analyze the most intense oceanic conditions off the UK and off New Zealand. The findings off the UK reveal that peak values off the UK and off the Irish coast tend to occur together, whereas they do not occur together at peak values at the Dover Strait. The model is then used to analyze data off New Zealand, revealing that peak values there are well described by a linearity relationship between time series.

Let $k$ be a number field and $C$ a smooth, projective, geometrically connected curve that isn't just points. Theorem 1 states that for any non-constant map $f$ from $C$ to a variety $X$ defined over $k$, there are only finitely many such maps up to composition with the Galois group of $k$ over $k$. This generalizes earlier results by Easton, Ferretti, and Stoll for the case when $C$ is the projective line. Furthermore, we examine the applicability of Theorem 1 to non-constant maps from $C$ to high-dimensional varieties, such as abelian varieties, and jet spaces, and consider the implications of these results in studying regluing techniques for curves.

Robot operators typically learn and apply their knowledge within a restricted area of the robot's workspace, known as the operability domain. To expand an operator's comfort and performance beyond this area, we propose a method for transferring the cobot's operability domain from one area of the workspace to another. The approach preserves the robot's safety and control properties, allowing the operator to retain their familiar interaction style while exploring previously uncharted areas. The proposed method involves two key steps: first, mapping the unexplored area to the known domain using feature-based ICP, and then mapping it back using a weighted iterative closest point approach that accounts for the geometry of both areas. The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated by mapping a human shoulder's operability domain onto a unexplored region above the shoulder.

A critical component of the Standard Model, the mechanism responsible for generating particle masses is also directly influenced. Therefore, it is essential to study this mechanism thoroughly to fully understand the electroweak symmetry breaking process. Researchers aim to do this by studying double Higgs boson generation, specifically focusing on the electroweak channel of $\textrm{WW}^{*}$ and the top-quark induced QCD channel of $\textrm{bb}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$, in order to distinguish between the two. This study examines double Higgs boson generation via matrix element analysis of the electroweak channel, using events with significant missing transverse energy and characteristics of soft leptons from the virtual W boson decay. Additionally, the analysis explores the potential for setting limits on the signal and the possibility of discovering it in 35/fb of luminosity with the CMS detector, based on simulations that include both signal and background processes.

Our study introduces a novel unsupervised learning approach that enables objects to acquire 3D coordinate awareness of their unique features, even without being explicitly taught the meaning of the coordinates. This is achieved by exposing the objects to rotating turntables, allowing them to learn by watching the rotation and identifying the forward direction as the key reference point for the coordinate system. The objects learn to recognize the unique characteristics of the four possible views of the rotating scene, encoding the direction coordinates and ultimately forming a complete 3D representation of the scene. This approach yields high-quality 3D models of the rotating scenes, matching the performance of state-of-the-art supervised methods. Additionally, the generated models can be used to train a supervised depth estimation model, further demonstrating the approach's effectiveness in recovering 3D structure.

A new challenge has emerged in the area of misinformation detection: distinguishing between social media posts that accept, reject, or simply engage with content about the legitimacy of the COVID-19 vaccine. To address this challenge, we have introduced the acceptance rejection Faking Challenge (ARC-FakeCh) dataset, consisting of 5,302 Twitter posts extracted from 152 conversations. These posts are labeled according to their stance on the legitimacy of the vaccine, and we have developed corresponding sub-tasks for the challenge. To fulfill these sub-tasks, users must combine a classification regarding misinformation type with a separate classification of acceptance or rejection. Our experimental results show that our proposed ARC-FakeCh dataset outperforms existing datasets in terms of performance and reliability. Furthermore, existing GPT-2 models have demonstrated the ability to achieve the highest possible score on our new challenge.

A breakthrough technique has been developed to generate extremely short, isolated attosecond pulses using a two-color strong-field high-harmonic generation process. A novel approach based on the V-shaped trajectory of electrons in a driven three-atom model effectively achieves Isolated Attosecond Pulse Enhancement (IAPe). A coherent control strategy for isolated attosecond pulse trains (IAPts) in a two-color strong-field environment offers an alternative to the conventional three-atom train method. By applying a reverse electric field and a barrier suppression tunneling effect, a single atom model produces charge packets that recollide with the atom and emit an IAPe. By adjusting the phase of the coherent emission, control over the attosecond pulse train amplitude and central wavelength can be achieved. Additionally, adjusting the phase of the coherent superposition of charge recollision can produce multi-pulse attosecond pulse trains with controllable characteristics.

We've conducted comprehensive spectroscopic and photometric observations of Algye 2 using various telescopes, focusing on its elusive companion. Our data from high-resolution spectra and long-term observations, combined with existing Hubble Space Telescope data, led us to reject the previous claims of the companion's presence. Our high-resolution spectra revealed no significant radial velocity changes, and our new observations match previous HST findings. Furthermore, our new ground-based data, along with old data, show no long-term radial velocity variations, indicating that Algye 2 remains a single star system. Additionally, our new high-resolution spectra require a 3D radiative atmosphere model to accurately determine the effective temperature, log(g), and microturbulence velocity. Our revised stellar parameters for the main star are Teff = 5900 K, log(g) = 4.34, and vt = 2.00 km/s, which, however, are inconsistent with its F8 spectral type and F8 IV luminosity class.

This paper focuses on determining the minimum mass threshold for the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, given by $i \psi_{t} + \Delta \psi - |\psi|^{2}\psi = 0$, outside of a bounded, smooth-shaped obstacle with the property of convexity. We are interested in finding the functional connection between this minimum mass and the curvature of the obstacle at its most sharply bent point. It is demonstrated that for any convex-shaped obstacle, the critical mass is lower than the numerically calculated value of $1.006...$ that had been previously estimated, and this new result is achieved through the use of a non-linear version of the Rayleigh-Dalton law. Additionally, we obtain estimates for the lower critical mass in the specific case of the spherical obstacle, which has the highest curvature.

PhysicsexplainingINNs, specificallyexplainingINNs, have significant applications where their output must match predefined model parameters, like material stiffness. Traditional optimization methods can incorporate physics into INN training but require extensive computational time. To address this issue, we introduce Residualbased Adaptative Gridcreation Method forINNs, or RANG, which dynamically adds material points during optimization based on two criteria: high physics residual and low sensitivity. This method ensures that material points are placed where they contribute most to improving physics consistency. We demonstrate RANG's effectiveness in a stiffness identification problem in 2D elasticity by comparing its results to an analytically determined solution.

In this research, the physics, design, and performance simulation of a multi-domain ferroelectric FET (FeFET) are explored. A key discovery is that the presence of domain walls in multilayer ferroelectric films results in a reduced effective dielectric constant in the channel area near these domain walls. This phenomenon significantly impacts the dielectric properties of FeFETs and must be considered in future device simulations. A novel approach for modeling FeFETs incorporating this effect is presented, incorporating a thermally-driven ferroelectric hysteresis model into a drift-diffusion simulator. By accounting for adverse capacitance near domain walls, the switching voltage of FeFETs increases by over 20%, and memory retention decreases. Thus, the adverse capacitance associated with domain walls in multi-domain FeFETs substantially influences their functionality.

The complex freight supply chain relies on a vast network of interconnected companies, and the performance of the entire system is significantly impacted by the struggles of individual firms within it. Identifying and understanding weaknesses in freight companies and their propagation throughout the supply chain is crucial for detecting and addressing potential risks. A data-driven method for detecting weaknesses in freight companies and analyzing their propagation among companies with comparable functions but different names is proposed. The Francine project, a part of the Francine European initiative, involved in standardizing freight services and processes, provided real-world data on freight companies in Europe. This initiative, along with additional publicly available data, was utilized to develop a weakly-supervised learning model, which employs a weakly-supervised learning approach, based on graph neural networks, to identify weaknesses in freight companies and analyze their propagation among these firms. The developed model demonstrates an accuracy of approximately 85% in classifying freight company weaknesses and has achieved a 0.6444 F1-score for weak propagations, outperforming model-based and similarity-based baselines by 10.5 and 10.2 percentage points respectively.

For analyzing ergodic properties in stochastic dynamical systems influenced by pure jump noises, it is crucial to establish irreducibility, which determines whether trajectories can reach any open set in the phase space. This study establishes a criterion for irreducibility in stochastic evolution equations and proves these findings for the complex Ginzburg-Landau equations with random jumps. Notably, the established irreducibility criterion is robust and, in some cases, reduces to simpler conditions when noises are additive or linear. Additionally, given the irreducibility criterion and the existence of random attractors, we demonstrate that ergodicity holds for stochastic CGL equations under pure jump noises.

Consider a finite group G and its power graph $\Gamma_G$, where vertices represent group elements with an edge connecting two vertices if one is a power of the other. For a given rational number $q$, we investigate power groups of groups G (not necessarily abelian) such that the quotient of the maximum to the minimum order of non-trivial elements in the power graph equals q. In this context, let $Nil_q$ be the maximum nilpotent order among groups satisfying this power graph element order condition. The aim is to find the smallest groups, in terms of size, that satisfy this power graph power order requirement for nilpotent groups. Specifically, for a p-group of a prime p, the power graph has a specific structure and this paper aims to identify the smallest groups of this power graph power order structure. The results of this paper show that a particular p-group of a specific order is the smallest p-group satisfying the power graph structure structure for a prime p and that a another particular p-group of a specific order is the smallest p-group satisfying the power graph structure structure for a prime p and a nilpotent number q.

A proposed advanced ADS (Advanced Detector System) is designed to take full advantage of the extra space available within the LHC's second iron bumper in forward BAMBOO, allowing for a significant expansion of its detection capabilities. By incorporating more advanced detectors and upgrading its calorimeter system, ADS can gather a wide array of data from various physics processes, including the investigation of the T-odd correlation in W-boson decays, in-search-for physics beyond the Standard Model in rare B-meson decays, the forward component of Higgs boson decays, the search for dark photons and colorons, the forward component of Charmonium decays, and the study of cosmic radiation in key areas, namely the Klein, Anderson-Higgs, and超子三体衰变 processes.

A new type of neural network, called Orientation Convolutive Networks (OCN), is proposed to handle spatial orientation in images in an implicit way. Unlike traditional neural networks that require extensive data with various orientation representations, OCN can implicitly learn spatial orientation invariance with minimally oriented data.
